grammar.title: Present perfect
grammar.lead: The present perfect links the past and the present. We use it for life experiences (without saying exactly when), recent actions with a present result, and situations that started in the past and continue now.

leadTr.uz: Present perfect o'tmish bilan hozirgi zamonni bog'laydi: hayotiy tajriba (qachonligini aytmasdan), natijasi hozir sezilib turgan yaqin voqealar uchun ishlatiladi.
leadTr.ru: Present perfect связывает прошлое с настоящим: жизненный опыт (без указания времени) и недавние действия с результатом в настоящем.

grammar.situation: “I have visited London twice.” We don’t say when — the experience matters now, not the exact time.

p: Use have (I/you/we/they) or has (he/she/it) + the past participle (the 3rd form: done, gone, seen, been).
ex: I have seen that film. · She has finished her work.

p: Use ever in questions and never in negatives to talk about experiences at any time in your life.
ex: Have you ever been to London? · I have never eaten sushi.

p: just = a very short time ago; already = sooner than expected; yet = used in questions and negatives at the end.
ex: I’ve just arrived. · She’s already left. · Have you finished yet?

p: Use for + a period of time and since + a point in time for situations continuing now.
ex: We’ve lived here for five years. · I’ve known him since 2018.

grammar.tip: Don’t use the present perfect with a finished past time. Say ‘I saw her yesterday’ (past simple), not ‘I have seen her yesterday’. Use the present perfect when the time is unfinished or unstated.
examples: "I have visited three countries."
"Have you ever ridden a horse?"
"She has never tried Italian food."
"We’ve just finished dinner."
"He has already done his homework."
"They’ve lived here for ten years."

mistakes.v: I saw him yesterday. (definite time → past simple)
She has gone home. (past participle)
I have been here since Monday.

quiz.q: I ___ my homework. (it's finished now)
She ___ to Paris. (experience)
The past participle of 'see' is ___.
We ___ this film before.
They ___ just arrived.
Have you ___ been to Spain?
quiz.e: In questions about experience we use ‘ever’.

quiz.q: I've ___ eaten octopus. (not in my life)
Has she finished ___?
quiz.e: In questions, ‘yet’ goes at the end.

quiz.q: We've lived here ___ 2015.
I've known him ___ ten years.
quiz.e: A period of time → for ten years.

quiz.q: Find the mistake: 'I have seen her yesterday.'
quiz.e: With ‘yesterday’ (finished time) use past simple: I saw her yesterday.

quiz.q: Complete: 'She ___ already ___ the email.'
Which is correct?
quiz.e: ‘yet’ goes at the end of the question.

quiz.q: Complete: 'I ___ this book ___ three days, but I haven't finished it.'
The past participle of 'go' (experience: visit and return) is ___.
quiz.e: For an experience there and back we use ‘been’: I have been to Rome.

grammar.title: Future: will & going to
grammar.lead: English has several ways to talk about the future. The two most common at A2 are ‘will’ and ‘be going to’. Each fits different situations — predictions, decisions, plans and intentions.

leadTr.uz: Ingliz tilida kelasi zamonni aytishning bir necha yo'li bor. A2 darajasida eng muhimlari — 'will' va 'be going to'; biri bashorat va qarorlar, ikkinchisi rejalar uchun.
leadTr.ru: В английском несколько способов говорить о будущем. На A2 главные — will и be going to: предсказания и решения против планов.

p: Use will + base verb for instant decisions, offers, promises and general predictions. Short form: ’ll; negative: won’t.
ex: I’ll help you. · It will rain tomorrow. · I won’t be late.

p: Use be going to + base verb for plans you have already decided and for predictions based on what you can see now.
ex: We’re going to visit Rome. · Look at the sky — it’s going to rain.

p: A decision made now = will; a plan decided before = going to.
ex: (phone rings) I’ll get it! · I’m going to study tonight. (already planned)

p: For fixed arrangements with a time, the present continuous is also common.
ex: I’m meeting Sara at six. · We’re flying on Monday.

grammar.tip: For a decision you make while speaking, use will: ‘I’ll have the chicken, please.’ For something you already planned, use going to: ‘I’m going to start a new job.’
examples: "I think it will be sunny tomorrow."
"Don’t worry, I ’ll carry that bag for you."
"We ’re going to buy a new car next month."
"Look out — you ’re going to drop it!"
"She won’t come to the meeting."
"I ’m meeting the doctor at 3 pm."

mistakes.v: I will call you. (will + base verb)

mistakes.x: Look at the clouds — it will rain.
mistakes.v: …it’s going to rain. (evidence now → going to)

quiz.q: I think it ___ rain tomorrow.
We ___ visit our grandparents next week. (a plan)
quiz.e: A decided plan → are going to visit.

quiz.q: The negative of 'will' is ___.
(The phone rings.) I ___ answer it!
quiz.e: An instant decision → I’ll answer it.

quiz.q: Look at those clouds! It ___ rain.
quiz.e: Prediction from evidence → is going to rain.

quiz.q: She ___ be twelve next month.
They ___ move to a new house. (already decided)
quiz.e: A plan → are going to move.

quiz.q: I promise I ___ tell anyone.
What ___ you ___ do at the weekend? (plans)
quiz.e: Asking about plans → are you going to do?

quiz.q: Choose the instant decision.
Find the mistake: 'I will to call you later.'
quiz.e: After ‘will’ use the base verb: I will call you.

quiz.q: Complete: 'A: I'm cold. B: I ___ close the window.'
quiz.e: Reacting now (offer) → I’ll close the window.

quiz.q: Which shows a fixed arrangement?
quiz.e: Arrangement with a time → present continuous.

quiz.q: Complete: 'We ___ (plan) start a business, and we hope it ___ (prediction) succeed.'
o: are going to / are going to
quiz.e: Plan → going to start; prediction → will succeed.

quiz.q: Choose the correct prediction from evidence.
o: She will have a baby — look!
She's going to have a baby — look!
She will to have a baby.
quiz.e: Evidence-based prediction → is going to have.

grammar.title: Comparatives & superlatives
grammar.lead: We use comparatives to compare two things and superlatives to compare one thing with all the others in a group. The form depends on the length of the adjective.

leadTr.uz: Comparative ikki narsani, superlative esa bir narsani guruhdagi barcha narsalar bilan solishtiradi. Shakl sifatning uzunligiga bog'liq: -er/-est yoki more/most.
leadTr.ru: Сравнительная степень сравнивает два предмета, превосходная — один предмет со всеми. Форма зависит от длины прилагательного: -er/-est или more/most.

p: One-syllable adjectives: add -er (comparative) and -est (superlative). Double a final consonant after a short vowel; -y becomes -ier/-iest.
ex: tall → taller → the tallest · big → bigger · happy → happier

p: Two or more syllables: use more (comparative) and the most (superlative).
ex: expensive → more expensive → the most expensive

p: Use than after a comparative, and the before a superlative.
ex: She is taller than me. · It’s the biggest city in the country.

p: A few adjectives are irregular.
ex: good → better → the best · bad → worse → the worst · far → further

grammar.tip: Don’t mix the two forms: ‘more taller’ and ‘most biggest’ are wrong. Use either -er/-est or more/most, never both.
examples: "Today is hotter than yesterday."
"This is the cheapest phone in the shop."
"Maths is more difficult than art for me."
"She is the most intelligent student in the class."
"My new car is better than my old one."
"It was the worst film I’ve ever seen."

mistakes.x: She is more taller than me.
mistakes.v: She is taller than me. (don’t use “more” with -er)
It is the biggest. (short adjective → -est)
He is better. (irregular)

quiz.q: This box is ___ than that one.
He is the ___ boy in the class.
quiz.e: Superlative of a short adjective: the tallest.

quiz.q: A car is ___ than a bicycle.
The comparative of 'big' is ___.
Gold is ___ than silver.
This is the ___ restaurant in town.
Today is ___ than yesterday.
The superlative of 'happy' is ___.
She is ___ student in the school.
quiz.e: Long adjective superlative: the most intelligent.

quiz.q: My bag is ___ than yours.
Find the mistake: 'This is more cheaper than that.'
Complete: 'It is ___ city ___ the country.'
quiz.e: Superlative: the biggest city in the country.

quiz.q: Which is correct?
Complete: 'This exam was ___ than the last one, but not ___ I've ever taken.'
quiz.e: more difficult than … the most difficult.

quiz.q: Choose the correct sentence.
o: My results are gooder than his.
My results are better than his.
My results are more good than his.
My results are best than his.

grammar.title: Adverbs of manner
grammar.lead: Adverbs of manner tell us how an action is done. They usually describe a verb and most are formed from adjectives.

leadTr.uz: Ravish (adverb of manner) ish-harakat qanday bajarilishini bildiradi. Ko'pchiligi sifatga -ly qo'shib yasaladi: slow → slowly.
leadTr.ru: Наречия образа действия говорят, как совершается действие. Большинство образуется от прилагательных с -ly: slow → slowly.

p: Most adverbs add -ly to the adjective. Adjectives ending in -y change to -ily; -le changes to -ly.
ex: slow → slowly · happy → happily · simple → simply

p: Some adverbs are irregular or the same as the adjective.
ex: good → well · fast → fast · hard → hard · early → early

p: The adverb usually goes after the verb (or after the object).
ex: She sings beautifully. · He drives the car carefully.

p: An adjective describes a noun; an adverb describes a verb.
ex: He is a careful driver. (adjective) · He drives carefully. (adverb)

grammar.tip: ‘Good’ is an adjective; its adverb is well: ‘She is a good singer’ but ‘She sings well.’ ‘She sings good’ is wrong.
examples: "He speaks English fluently."
"Please drive slowly."
"She plays the piano well."
"They worked hard all day."
"The children played happily in the garden."
"He answered the question correctly."

mistakes.v: He speaks English very well. (good → well)
She sings beautifully. (verb → adverb)

quiz.q: She sings ___.
The adverb of 'quick' is ___.
He runs very ___.
quiz.e: ‘fast’ is the same as adverb and adjective.

quiz.q: Please speak ___.
The adverb of 'good' is ___.
They worked ___ all day.
quiz.e: ‘hard’ (= with effort) is the adverb; ‘hardly’ means ‘almost not’.

quiz.q: She plays the violin ___.
The adverb of 'happy' is ___.
He drives ___.
Choose the adverb sentence.
Find the mistake: 'He sings very good.'
quiz.e: Use the adverb ‘well’: He sings very well.

quiz.q: Complete: 'She is a ___ worker and she works ___.'
Which is correct?
quiz.e: Adverb after the object: answered the question correctly.

quiz.q: Complete: 'The test was ___, so she finished it ___.'
Choose the correct adverb form.

grammar.title: Quantifiers: much, many, a lot of
grammar.lead: Quantifiers say how much or how many. The right one depends on whether the noun is countable or uncountable, and whether the sentence is positive, negative or a question.

leadTr.uz: Miqdor so'zlari (much, many, a lot of) qancha ekanini bildiradi. To'g'ri tanlov ot sanaladigan yoki sanalmaydigan ekaniga bog'liq.
leadTr.ru: Кванторы (much, many, a lot of) выражают количество. Правильный выбор зависит от того, исчисляемое существительное или нет.

p: Use many with countable nouns and much with uncountable nouns, mostly in questions and negatives.
ex: How many apples? · How much water? · I don’t have much time.

p: Use a lot of (or lots of) with both countable and uncountable nouns, usually in positive sentences.
ex: She has a lot of friends. · We have a lot of homework.

p: Use a few with countable nouns and a little with uncountable nouns to mean ‘a small amount’.
ex: I have a few questions. · Add a little salt.

p: too much/many = more than you want; enough = the right amount.
ex: There are too many cars. · We don’t have enough chairs.

grammar.tip: In positive sentences, a lot of usually sounds better than ‘much’ or ‘many’: say ‘I have a lot of work’, not ‘I have much work’.
examples: "How many students are in your class?"
"There isn’t much milk left."
"We have a lot of homework today."
"I only need a few minutes."
"Add a little sugar to the tea."
"There are too many people here."

mistakes.v: How many books? (countable → many)
I have a lot of money. (uncountable, positive → a lot of)

quiz.q: How ___ apples do you want?
How ___ water is there?
She has ___ friends.
I have ___ books on this subject.
Add ___ salt to the soup.
There isn't ___ time left.
We don't have ___ chairs.
There are ___ people in the room. (more than we want)
I'd like ___ sugar in my coffee.
We have ___ homework tonight.
Find the mistake: 'I have much friends.'
quiz.e: Countable positive → ‘many’ or ‘a lot of’ friends.

quiz.q: Complete: 'There isn't ___ juice, but there are ___ apples.'
Which is correct?
o: We don't have a enough chairs.
quiz.e: ‘enough’ goes before the noun: enough chairs.

quiz.q: Complete: 'How ___ money do you need? Only ___.'
Choose the natural sentence.
o: He drinks a lot of coffee.
quiz.e: Positive + uncountable → a lot of coffee.

grammar.title: Verb + infinitive or -ing
grammar.lead: After certain verbs we use the infinitive (to + verb); after others we use the -ing form. Learning which verbs take which form is an important A2 skill.

leadTr.uz: Ba'zi fe'llardan keyin infinitiv (to + fe'l), boshqalaridan keyin -ing shakli keladi: want to go, lekin enjoy going. Qaysi fe'l qaysi shaklni olishini yodlash kerak.
leadTr.ru: После одних глаголов идёт инфинитив (to + глагол), после других — форма -ing: want to go, но enjoy going. Какой глагол что требует — нужно запомнить.

p: These verbs are followed by to + base verb: want, would like, need, decide, hope, plan, promise, learn, try.
ex: I want to go home. · She decided to stay. · We hope to win.

p: These verbs are followed by the -ing form: like, love, enjoy, hate, finish, stop, mind, suggest, practise.
ex: I enjoy reading. · They finished eating. · Do you mind waiting?

p: Use to + verb to explain why you do something (the purpose).
ex: I went to the shop to buy milk.

p: like + -ing = enjoy in general; would like + to = want now.
ex: I like swimming. · I’d like to swim now.

grammar.tip: Memorise verbs in short phrases: ‘want to go’, ‘enjoy going’. When unsure, remember that want, need, hope and decide take to, while enjoy, finish and stop take -ing.
examples: "I want to learn Spanish."
"She enjoys cooking for her family."
"They decided to move to a new city."
"He finished doing his homework."
"We went out to celebrate her birthday."
"Do you mind opening the window?"

mistakes.v: I want to go home. (want + to)
I enjoy swimming. (enjoy + -ing)

quiz.q: I want ___ home.
She enjoys ___.
We hope ___ the match.
They finished ___ dinner.
I need ___ a doctor.
He decided ___ at home.
Do you mind ___ the door?
I went to the library ___ a book.
She stopped ___ because she was tired.
We learned ___ in summer.
Find the mistake: 'I enjoy to read books.'
Complete: 'She wants ___ a teacher, so she's learning ___ children.'
quiz.e: want + to (to become); learn + to (but here ‘teaching’ as a noun-like activity she practises) → best: to teach. (to become / to teach)

quiz.q: Which is correct?
quiz.e: would like + to: I’d like to swim.

quiz.q: Complete: 'He finished ___ and then decided ___ for a walk.'
Choose the purpose sentence.
o: I study to passing the exam.
I study to pass the exam.
I study for pass the exam.
quiz.e: Purpose uses to + base verb: to pass.

grammar.title: Present perfect vs past simple
grammar.lead: These two tenses both talk about the past, but they are used differently. The past simple is for a finished time; the present perfect connects the past to now.

leadTr.uz: Ikkala zamon ham o'tmish haqida, lekin: past simple — tugagan vaqt uchun (yesterday, in 2020), present perfect esa o'tmishni hozir bilan bog'laydi.
leadTr.ru: Оба времени о прошлом, но past simple — для законченного времени (yesterday, in 2020), а present perfect связывает прошлое с настоящим.

p: Use the past simple with a finished time word (yesterday, last week, in 2010). Use the present perfect when the time is unstated or unfinished (today, this week, ever).
ex: I saw her yesterday. · I have seen that film. (when? not important)

p: Present perfect = experience at any time. Past simple = a specific completed event.
ex: Have you ever been to Rome? — Yes, I went there in 2019.

p: Present perfect shows a present result; past simple just reports a finished action.
ex: I’ve lost my keys. (I can’t find them now) · I lost my keys yesterday.

p: Past simple: yesterday, ago, last…, in 2015. Present perfect: ever, never, just, already, yet, recently, since, for.
ex: She moved here two years ago. · She has lived here for two years.

grammar.tip: A finished time word forces the past simple. ‘I have finished it yesterday’ is wrong → ‘I finished it yesterday.’
examples: "I have visited Paris, but I visited it last spring."
"She has just left."
"They arrived two hours ago."
"Have you ever eaten sushi? — Yes, I tried it in Tokyo."
"We have known each other since 2018."
"He didn’t call me yesterday."

mistakes.v: I finished it yesterday. (yesterday = finished time)
Have you ever eaten sushi? (life experience → present perfect)

quiz.q: I ___ my homework yesterday.
She ___ to Japan. (experience)
We ___ a great film last night.
He ___ his keys. (he can't find them now)
They ___ here in 2015.
___ you ever ___ a horse?
quiz.e: Experience question → Have you ever ridden?

quiz.q: I ___ him two days ago.
She's not here; she ___ already ___.
We ___ in this town for ten years.
quiz.e: ‘for ten years’ continuing → present perfect: have lived.

quiz.q: What time ___ you ___ home last night?
quiz.e: ‘last night’ → past simple: did you arrive?

quiz.q: Find the mistake: 'I have seen her last week.'
quiz.e: ‘last week’ forces past simple: I saw her last week.

quiz.q: Complete: 'I ___ Tom for years. We ___ at school in 2010.'
Which is correct?
o: Did you ever go to Spain?
Have you ever been to Spain?
Have you ever went to Spain?
Did you ever been to Spain?

quiz.q: Complete: 'She ___ three books this year, and she ___ this one last weekend.'
Choose the sentence with a present result.
o: I've broken my arm — it hurts!
quiz.e: Present perfect shows the result now: I’ve broken my arm.

grammar.title: used to
grammar.lead: We use ‘used to’ to talk about past habits and states that are no longer true. It is a simple way to contrast the past with the present.

leadTr.uz: 'Used to' endi mavjud bo'lmagan o'tmishdagi odat va holatlarni bildiradi: I used to play football — ilgari o'ynardim (hozir yo'q).
leadTr.ru: Used to описывает прошлые привычки и состояния, которых больше нет: I used to play football — раньше играл (теперь нет).

grammar.situation: “I used to play tennis, but I stopped years ago.” — used to describes a past habit or state that is no longer true.

p: used to + base verb describes something that happened regularly in the past, or a state that was true before but isn’t now.
ex: I used to play football every day. · She used to live in Leeds.

p: Negative: didn’t use to (no -d). Question: Did … use to…?
ex: He didn’t use to like coffee. · Did you use to have long hair?

p: ‘used to’ always contrasts the past with now.
ex: I used to smoke, but now I don’t. · We didn’t use to have a car, but now we do.

p: For present habits, use the present simple, not ‘used to’.
ex: Now I go to the gym every day. (not ‘I use to go’)

grammar.tip: In negatives and questions the ‘-d’ disappears: ‘didn’t use to’ and ‘Did you use to…?’, never ‘didn’t used to’.
examples: "I used to live in a small village."
"She used to have long hair."
"We didn’t use to watch much TV."
"Did you use to walk to school?"
"He used to be shy, but now he’s very confident."
"They used to play outside every afternoon."

mistakes.v: I used to live here. (affirmative: used)
I didn’t use to smoke. (after did → use, no -d)

quiz.q: I ___ play tennis when I was young.
She ___ live in London.
We ___ have a dog.
They ___ go to the beach every summer.
He ___ be very thin.
Negative: 'I ___ like vegetables.'
quiz.e: Negative drops the -d: didn’t use to.

quiz.q: ___ you use to have long hair?
She ___ like coffee, but now she loves it.
quiz.e: Negative past habit: didn’t use to.

quiz.q: We ___ play outside, but now we stay in.
Choose the correct question.
quiz.e: Did + use to (no -d): Did you use to smoke?

quiz.q: Find the mistake: 'He didn't used to study hard.'
o: didn't used to → didn't use to
quiz.e: Drop the -d after didn’t: didn’t use to study.

quiz.q: Complete: 'I ___ be afraid of dogs, but now I ___ them.'
Which sentence is correct for a present habit?
o: Now I use to run daily.
Now I used to run daily.
Now I am use to run daily.
quiz.e: For present habits use the present simple: I run daily.

quiz.q: Complete: '___ they ___ live near here?'
quiz.e: Did + use to: Did they use to live…?

quiz.q: Choose the natural contrast.
o: I used to play piano, and I still do every day exactly the same.
I used to play piano, but I stopped years ago.
I use to play piano now.
I am used to play piano before.
quiz.e: ‘used to’ contrasts a past habit with the present (now stopped).

grammar.title: Obligation: must, have to, should
grammar.lead: These modal verbs talk about rules, necessity and advice. ‘Must’ and ‘have to’ express obligation; ‘should’ gives advice; their negatives have different meanings.

leadTr.uz: Bu modal fe'llar qoida, zarurat va maslahatni bildiradi: 'must' va 'have to' — majburiyat, 'should' — maslahat. Inkor shakllari esa turlicha ma'no beradi.
leadTr.ru: Эти модальные глаголы выражают правила, необходимость и совет: must и have to — обязанность, should — совет. Их отрицания означают разное.

p: must and have to + base verb both mean something is necessary. ‘Must’ often comes from the speaker; ‘have to’ often comes from outside rules.
ex: You must wear a seatbelt. · I have to work on Saturday.

p: should + base verb gives advice or an opinion about the best thing to do.
ex: You should see a doctor. · We shouldn’t waste food.

p: mustn’t = it is prohibited (don’t do it!). don’t have to = it isn’t necessary (but you can).
ex: You mustn’t smoke here. (forbidden) · You don’t have to come. (optional)

p: The past of both ‘must’ and ‘have to’ is had to.
ex: Yesterday I had to stay late at work.

grammar.tip: Be careful: mustn’t and don’t have to are very different. ‘You mustn’t go’ = do NOT go. ‘You don’t have to go’ = you can stay if you like.
examples: "You must stop at a red light."
"I have to get up early tomorrow."
"You should drink more water."
"You mustn’t use your phone in the exam."
"We don’t have to pay — it’s free."
"She had to wait an hour for the bus."

mistakes.x: You mustn’t pay — it’s free, so it’s OK not to.
mistakes.v: You don’t have to pay. (no obligation ≠ mustn’t)
He must go. (must + base verb)

quiz.q: You ___ wear a uniform at this school. (rule)
You look tired. You ___ go to bed.
You ___ smoke here. It's forbidden.
I ___ get up early tomorrow.
We ___ waste water.
It's free, so you ___ pay.
Students ___ be quiet in the library. (rule)
The past of 'I must leave' is ___.
quiz.e: Past of must/have to → had to leave.

quiz.q: You're ill. You ___ see a doctor.
You ___ touch that — it's dangerous!
Find the difference: 'You don't have to come.' means ___.
Complete: 'You ___ be late, but you ___ come if you're busy.'
Which gives advice correctly?
quiz.e: should + base verb: You should study more.

quiz.q: Complete: 'Yesterday I ___ work late, so I ___ cancel my plans.'
Choose the prohibition.
o: You don't have to park here.

grammar.title: First conditional
grammar.lead: The first conditional talks about a real or likely situation in the future and its result. It uses ‘if’ + present simple for the condition and ‘will’ for the result.

leadTr.uz: Birinchi shart gapi (first conditional) kelajakdagi real vaziyat va uning natijasini bildiradi: If + present simple, natijada esa 'will'.
leadTr.ru: Первый кондиционал описывает реальную будущую ситуацию и её результат: if + present simple, а в результате — will.

grammar.situation: “If it rains tomorrow, we ’ll stay at home.” — The first conditional talks about a real, likely future result.

p: The if-clause uses the present simple; the result clause uses will + base verb.
ex: If it rains, we will stay home.
I will call you if I have time.

p: You can start with either clause. Use a comma only when the if-clause comes first.
ex: If you study, you’ll pass. · You’ll pass if you study.

p: unless means ‘if … not’.
ex: You’ll be late unless you hurry. (= if you don’t hurry)

blocks.h: may / might / can in the result
p: Instead of ‘will’, you can use may, might (possible) or can (ability) in the result.
ex: If it’s sunny, we might go to the beach.

grammar.tip: Don’t use ‘will’ in the if-clause: ‘If it will rain’ is wrong → ‘If it rains, we will stay home.’ The condition is in the present simple.
examples: "If it rains, we will stay at home."
"If you heat ice, it melts."
"I’ll help you if you ask me."
"You’ll miss the bus unless you run."
"If she studies hard, she will pass."
"If we leave now, we might catch the train."

mistakes.x: If it will rain, I will stay in.
mistakes.v: If it rains, I will stay in. (no “will” after if)
If you study, you ’ll pass.

quiz.q: If it rains, we ___ at home.
If you ___ hard, you'll pass.
I'll call you if I ___ time.
If she runs, she ___ the bus.
We'll have a picnic if the weather ___ nice.
If you ___ now, you'll arrive on time.
You'll be tired ___ you sleep more.
If I ___ the exam, my parents will be happy.
If it's sunny, we ___ go to the park.
Choose the correct sentence.
o: If it will rain, I'll stay.

quiz.q: Find the mistake: 'If you will help me, I'll finish faster.'
quiz.e: No ‘will’ in the if-clause: If you help me…

quiz.q: Complete: 'You ___ pass ___ you study harder.'
quiz.e: ‘won’t pass unless you study’ = if you don’t study.

quiz.q: Which is correct?
o: If we leave now, we catch the train.
If we leave now, we'll catch the train.
If we will leave now, we'll catch.
If we leave now, we caught the train.

quiz.q: Complete: 'If it ___ tomorrow, the match ___ cancelled.'
Choose the sentence with correct punctuation.
o: You'll be fine, if you relax.
If you relax you'll be fine.
If you relax, you'll be fine.
If, you relax you'll be fine.
quiz.e: Comma after the if-clause when it comes first.

grammar.title: Relative clauses
grammar.lead: Relative clauses give extra information about a noun. They begin with a relative pronoun — who, which, that, where — and help you build longer, more natural sentences.

leadTr.uz: Nisbiy ergash gaplar (relative clauses) ot haqida qo'shimcha ma'lumot beradi. Ular who, which, that, where bilan boshlanadi va uzunroq, tabiiyroq gaplar qurishga yordam beradi.
leadTr.ru: Относительные придаточные дают дополнительную информацию о существительном. Они начинаются с who, which, that, where и делают речь естественнее.

p: Use who for people and which for things and animals.
ex: The man who lives next door is a doctor.
I bought a phone which takes great photos.

p: that can replace who or which in many sentences, especially in speaking.
ex: The book that I read was excellent.

p: Use where to talk about a place.
ex: This is the café where we first met.

p: Use whose to show that something belongs to someone.
ex: That’s the girl whose brother is a singer.

grammar.tip: Use who for people, which for things; that can replace either. Don’t add an extra pronoun: ‘The man who he lives next door’ is wrong — drop ‘he’.
examples: "The woman who teaches us is very kind."
"This is the laptop which I bought yesterday."
"He’s the player that scored the goal."
"That’s the town where I was born."
"She’s the friend whose car we borrowed."
"The film that we saw was boring."

mistakes.v: The man who called… (people → who)

mistakes.x: That’s the house which I live.
mistakes.v: That’s the house where I live. (place → where)

quiz.q: The man ___ lives here is my uncle.
I have a watch ___ was very expensive.
This is the school ___ I study.
She's the woman ___ son is a doctor.
The book ___ I read was great.
The teacher ___ teaches English is new.
That's the restaurant ___ we had dinner.
I like the shoes ___ you're wearing.
He's the boy ___ won the competition.
Choose the correct relative pronoun: 'a person ___ helps others.'
Find the mistake: 'The man who he lives next door is friendly.'
quiz.e: Don’t add an extra subject: The man who lives next door…

quiz.q: Complete: 'That's the girl ___ bag was stolen and ___ called the police.'
Which is correct?
o: The film who we saw was good.
The film which we saw was good.
The film where we saw was good.
The film whose we saw was good.

quiz.q: Complete: 'This is the hospital ___ I was born, near the park ___ is now closed.'
quiz.e: Place ‘where I was born’ + thing ‘which is now closed’.

quiz.q: Choose the natural sentence.
o: I know a place that sells great coffee.
I know a place who sells great coffee.
I know a place whose sells great coffee.
I know a place where sells great coffee.

grammar.title: Linking words: because, so, but, although
grammar.lead: Linking words join ideas to make your writing and speaking flow. They show reasons, results, contrasts and additions between two parts of a sentence.

leadTr.uz: Bog'lovchi so'zlar (because, so, but, although) fikrlarni bir-biriga bog'laydi: sabab, natija, qarama-qarshilik va qo'shimchani ko'rsatadi.
leadTr.ru: Союзы because, so, but, although связывают идеи: причина, следствие, контраст и дополнение между частями предложения.

p: because introduces a reason; so introduces a result.
ex: I stayed home because I was ill. · I was ill, so I stayed home.

p: but joins two contrasting ideas in one sentence; however often starts a new sentence.
ex: It was cold, but we went out. · It was cold. However, we went out.

p: although introduces a surprising contrast within a sentence.
ex: Although it was raining, we played football.

p: and adds; or gives a choice; also adds extra information.
ex: We had tea and cake. · Tea or coffee? · She sings; she also dances.

grammar.tip: ‘because’ is followed by a reason and ‘so’ by a result. ‘I was tired because I worked late’ = the reason; ‘I worked late, so I was tired’ = the result.
examples: "I was hungry, so I made a sandwich."
"She passed because she studied hard."
"He’s rich, but he isn’t happy."
"Although she was tired, she finished the work."
"Would you like tea or coffee?"
"It rained all day, so we stayed inside."

mistakes.x: Because it was late, so we left.
mistakes.v: Use one linker: Because it was late, we left. (not both)

mistakes.x: Although it was hard but he tried.
mistakes.v: Although it was hard, he tried. (no “but” with “although”)

quiz.q: I was tired, ___ I went to bed.
She was happy ___ she passed the exam.
It was raining, ___ we went out.
Would you like tea ___ coffee?
We had cake ___ ice cream.
___ it was cold, we went swimming.
He didn't study, ___ he failed.
I like coffee ___ I don't drink it at night.
They stayed home ___ the bad weather.
Choose the reason: 'We left early ___ the film was boring.'
Find the mistake: 'Although it was late, but we kept working.'
quiz.e: Don’t use ‘although’ and ‘but’ together: Although it was late, we kept working.

quiz.q: Complete: 'I was ill, ___ I missed school ___ I'm fine now.'
quiz.e: Result ‘so I missed school’ + contrast ‘but I’m fine now’.

quiz.q: Which sentence shows a contrast correctly?
o: Because it was hot, we wore coats.
Although it was hot, we wore coats.
So it was hot, we wore coats.
And it was hot, we wore coats.

quiz.q: Complete: 'She studied medicine ___ she wanted to help people, ___ now she's a doctor.'
quiz.e: Reason ‘because’ + addition ‘and now she’s a doctor’.

quiz.q: Choose the correct linker for a result.
o: It snowed heavily because the roads closed.
It snowed heavily, so the roads closed.
It snowed heavily although the roads closed.
It snowed heavily but the roads closed.

grammar.title: Question tags
grammar.lead: Question tags are short questions added to the end of a statement, used to check information or invite agreement. The tag matches the tense and reverses the verb.

leadTr.uz: Question tags — gap oxiriga qo'shiladigan qisqa savollar: ma'lumotni tekshirish yoki rozilik so'rash uchun. Tag zamonga mos keladi va fe'lni teskarisiga aylantiradi.
leadTr.ru: Разделительные вопросы — короткие вопросы в конце утверждения для проверки информации. Хвостик повторяет время и меняет утверждение на отрицание.

p: After a positive statement, the tag is negative, using the same auxiliary verb.
ex: You’re from Spain, aren’t you? · She likes tea, doesn’t she?

p: After a negative statement, the tag is positive.
ex: You aren’t tired, are you? · He didn’t call, did he?

p: Use ‘be’ with ‘be’; with other verbs use do/does/did; with the present perfect use have/has; with modals repeat the modal.
ex: They can swim, can’t they? · You’ve finished, haven’t you?

p: ‘I am’ → tag is aren’t I. ‘Let’s…’ → tag is shall we.
ex: I’m next, aren’t I? · Let’s go, shall we?

grammar.tip: The tag repeats the auxiliary verb and reverses positive/negative. Statement positive → tag negative, and the other way round: ‘He’s here, isn’t he?’ / ‘He isn’t here, is he?’
examples: "You’re a student, aren’t you?"
"She works here, doesn’t she?"
"They didn’t come, did they?"
"He can drive, can’t he?"
"We’ve met before, haven’t we?"
"Let’s have a break, shall we?"

mistakes.v: You’re ready, aren’t you? (match the verb & subject)
She can swim, can’t she? (positive → negative tag)

reading.title: A Trip to London
reading.text:
Last summer, Daniel and his sister Olivia travelled to London for the first time. They took an early train from Manchester and arrived at about ten o'clock.
First, they visited the British Museum, which was free and very interesting. After that, they had lunch in a small café near the river. In the afternoon, they went on a boat trip and saw many famous buildings.
The weather was warm and sunny all day. In the evening, they were tired but happy. They bought some souvenirs and took lots of photos before they caught the last train home.

quiz.e: They took a train from Manchester.

reading.title: My First Job
reading.text:
My name is Sophie and I'm nineteen. Last year, I got my first job in a small bookshop in Bristol. At first, I was nervous because I didn't have any experience.
My manager, Mr Clarke, was very kind and patient. He showed me how to use the till and how to help customers find books. The other staff were friendly too, so I soon felt comfortable.
I worked part-time, three days a week, and the salary wasn't very high. But I learned a lot, and I really enjoyed talking to customers about books. Now I want to study literature at university.

quiz.q: Where does Sophie work?
quiz.e: She works in a bookshop in Bristol.

quiz.e: She was nervous because she had no experience.

quiz.e: Mr Clarke was kind and patient.

quiz.e: She works part-time, three days a week.

quiz.e: She wants to study literature at university.

reading.title: An Email about a Holiday
reading.text:
Hi Grace,

How are you? I'm writing from a small hotel in Brighton, where I've been since Monday. I'm having a wonderful time!

I've already done so many things. I've walked along the beach, eaten fresh fish, and visited the famous pier. Yesterday I went swimming in the sea, although the water was quite cold. I haven't been shopping yet, but I'm planning to go tomorrow.

The weather has been mostly sunny, but it rained a little this morning. The people here are very friendly, and the food is delicious.

I'll be home on Saturday. Let's meet next week — I'll show you my photos!

Love,
Jack

quiz.e: He's in a small hotel in Brighton.

quiz.e: It rained a little this morning.

reading.title: Town or City?
reading.text:
Many people argue about whether it is better to live in a big city or a small town. Both have advantages and disadvantages.
Big cities, like London or Birmingham, are more exciting. There are more jobs, better shops, and lots of things to do in the evening. However, cities are usually more expensive and more crowded, and the air is often more polluted.
Small towns are quieter and cheaper. People are often friendlier and know their neighbours. On the other hand, there are fewer jobs, and young people sometimes find life a little boring.
In my opinion, the best choice depends on your age and your needs. When I was younger, I loved the city, but now I prefer the peace of a small town.

o: more jobs and things to do
quiz.e: Cities have more jobs and things to do.

quiz.q: What is one disadvantage of big cities?
quiz.e: Cities are more expensive and crowded.

quiz.q: According to the text, people in small towns are often ___.
quiz.e: People in small towns are often friendlier.

quiz.e: There are fewer jobs and less to do.

quiz.q: What does the writer prefer now?
o: the peace of a small town
quiz.e: Now the writer prefers the peace of a small town.

reading.title: The Lost Phone
reading.text:
It was a cold Friday evening, and Emily was hurrying home from work. While she was waiting at the bus stop, she took out her phone to check the time. The bus arrived, and in the rush to get on, she didn't notice that her phone had fallen onto the seat next to her.
When she got home, she realised her phone was missing. She felt terrible — all her photos and messages were on it. She borrowed her flatmate's phone and called her own number, but nobody answered.
The next morning, however, she received an email. A kind passenger named Harry had found the phone and seen her details on the screen. They arranged to meet at a café in the city centre, and Harry returned the phone. Emily was so grateful that she bought him a coffee. Now they are good friends.

quiz.q: What was Emily doing when she lost her phone?
quiz.e: She was hurrying home from work.

quiz.q: How did she lose the phone?
o: She dropped it in the street.
It fell onto the bus seat in the rush.
She left it at the office.
quiz.e: It fell onto the seat as she rushed onto the bus.

quiz.q: Why did she feel terrible?
o: All her photos and messages were on the phone.
quiz.e: Her photos and messages were on the phone.

quiz.q: How did Harry contact her?
o: He sent an email after seeing her details.
quiz.e: He emailed her after seeing her details on the screen.

quiz.q: What happened in the end?
o: Harry returned the phone and they became friends.
quiz.e: Harry returned it and now they are good friends.

grammar.title: Present perfect continuous
grammar.lead: The present perfect continuous links the past to the present and emphasises the duration or repetition of an activity, especially one that is still going on or has only just stopped.

leadTr.uz: Present perfect continuous o'tmishni hozir bilan bog'lab, harakatning davomiyligini ta'kidlaydi — ayniqsa hali davom etayotgan yoki endigina tugagan faoliyat uchun.
leadTr.ru: Present perfect continuous связывает прошлое с настоящим и подчёркивает длительность действия — особенно продолжающегося или только что закончившегося.

grammar.situation: “You look exhausted!” “Yes, I ’ve been working in the garden all day.” — The present perfect continuous focuses on an activity that has been going on and explains a present result.

p: Use have/has been + verb-ing. It focuses on the activity itself rather than the finished result.
ex: I have been working all day. · She has been studying since nine.

p: Use for + a period and since + a starting point to show how long the activity has lasted.
ex: We’ve been waiting for two hours. · He’s been living here since 2019.

p: The continuous stresses how long / how active; the simple stresses the completed result.
ex: I’ve been reading this book. (still reading) · I’ve read this book. (finished)

p: It can explain a present situation caused by a recent activity.
ex: You look tired. — Yes, I’ve been running.

grammar.tip: Don’t use the continuous with state verbs (know, like, be, have = possess): say ‘I have known her for years’, not ‘I have been knowing’.
examples: "I ’ve been learning English for five years."
"It has been raining all morning."
"They ’ve been working on the project since Monday."
"Why are you so dirty? — I ’ve been gardening."
"She ’s been feeling ill recently."
"We ’ve been waiting for ages."

mistakes.x: I have been knowing her for years.
mistakes.v: I have known her for years. (state verb → simple)

mistakes.x: I am working here since May.
mistakes.v: I ’ve been working here since May.

quiz.q: I ___ for two hours and I'm still not finished.
quiz.e: Ongoing activity + duration → have been working.

quiz.q: She ___ since this morning.
How long ___ you ___ here?
quiz.e: Duration of an ongoing situation → have you been living.

quiz.e: Activity with present result → has been raining.

quiz.e: Duration of activity → have been playing.

quiz.e: Recent activity explaining a state → have you been doing.

quiz.e: Both are possible, but with ‘since’ + ongoing the continuous is natural: has been living.

quiz.q: Which verb is wrong in the continuous?
quiz.e: ‘know’ is a state verb → not used in the continuous.

quiz.q: Complete: 'My eyes hurt because I ___ at the screen.'
quiz.e: Recent ongoing activity → have been staring.

quiz.q: Find the mistake: 'I have been knowing him for years.'
quiz.e: State verb: I have known him for years.

quiz.q: Complete: 'She ___ all morning, so the cake is ready.'
quiz.e: Activity over a period explaining a result → has been baking.

quiz.q: Which sentence stresses the finished result?
quiz.e: Completed result with a number → present perfect simple: I’ve written three emails.

quiz.q: Complete: 'They ___ in this town ___ ten years and they love it.'
quiz.e: Ongoing + period → have been living for ten years.

quiz.q: Choose the natural sentence.
o: How long have you been waiting?
How long have you waited continuously?
quiz.e: Duration of an ongoing wait → have you been waiting.

grammar.title: Past perfect
grammar.lead: The past perfect shows that one past action happened before another past action. It helps to make the order of events in a story clear.

leadTr.uz: Past perfect bir o'tmishdagi harakat boshqa o'tmishdagi harakatdan OLDIN bo'lganini ko'rsatadi. U hikoyada voqealar tartibini aniq qiladi.
leadTr.ru: Past perfect показывает, что одно прошлое действие произошло РАНЬШЕ другого. Он делает порядок событий в рассказе ясным.

grammar.situation: “When I got to the station, the train had already left.” — The past perfect shows the train left before I arrived. It puts two past events in order.

p: Use had + past participle for the earlier of two past actions.
ex: When I arrived, the train had already left.

p: Often used with the past simple: the past perfect = the earlier action; the past simple = the later one.
ex: She had finished dinner before he came home.

blocks.h: after, before, when, by the time
p: Common with these time linkers to show sequence.
ex: By the time we got there, the film had started.

p: Negative: hadn’t + past participle. Question: Had + subject + past participle?
ex: I hadn’t seen her before. · Had you eaten when they called?

grammar.tip: Use the past perfect only when you need to show one past event happened before another. For a simple sequence (first… then…), the past simple alone is enough.
examples: "When we arrived, the party had already started."
"She had never flown before that day."
"They had finished the work before the boss returned."
"By the time I woke up, he had left."
"I knew I had met him somewhere."
"Had you booked the room before you arrived?"

mistakes.x: After I had ate, I went out.
mistakes.v: After I had eaten, I went out. (past participle)

mistakes.x: When I arrived, the film already started.
mistakes.v: …the film had already started.

quiz.q: When I arrived, the train ___.
quiz.e: Earlier past action → had already left.

___ you ever ___ abroad before that holiday?
quiz.e: Past perfect question: Had you been?

quiz.q: Choose the earlier action: 'When I phoned, she ___.'
quiz.e: Before the phone call → had gone out.

quiz.q: Find the mistake: 'After I had ate, I went out.'
quiz.e: Past participle of eat is eaten: had eaten.

quiz.q: Complete: 'By the time the police arrived, the thief ___.'
Which order is correct?
o: He had left before I arrived.
He left before I had arrived.
He had left before I had arrived.

quiz.q: Complete: 'I didn't recognise the town because it ___ so much.'
Choose the natural sentence.
o: When the guests arrived, she had cooked dinner.
When the guests arrived, she has cooked dinner.
When the guests arrived, she cooks dinner.
When the guests had arrived, she has cooked.
quiz.e: Dinner cooked before guests arrived → had cooked.

grammar.title: Future forms
grammar.lead: English uses several forms to talk about the future. Choosing the right one depends on whether you mean a prediction, a plan, an arrangement, a timetable or an instant decision.

leadTr.uz: Kelasi zamonning bir necha shakli bor. To'g'ri tanlov nimani nazarda tutishingizga bog'liq: bashorat, reja, kelishuv, jadval yoki hozirgi qaror.
leadTr.ru: У будущего времени несколько форм. Выбор зависит от смысла: предсказание, план, договорённость, расписание или спонтанное решение.

p: will = predictions, instant decisions, offers, promises. be going to = plans/intentions and predictions from evidence.
ex: It will snow tonight. · We’re going to paint the house.

p: Use the present continuous for fixed arrangements, usually with a time and another person.
ex: I’m meeting Sara at six. · They’re flying to Rome on Friday.

p: Use the present simple for timetabled events (transport, programmes, schedules).
ex: The train leaves at 9:15. · The film starts at eight.

p: Use may/might for things that are possible but not certain.
ex: It might rain later. · I may go to the party.

grammar.tip: For a plan use ‘going to’; for an arrangement with a time use the present continuous; for a timetable use the present simple; for an instant decision use ‘will’.
examples: "Look at the clouds — it ’s going to rain."
"I think she ’ll pass the exam."
"We ’re having dinner with friends tonight."
"The bus leaves at half past seven."
"I might visit my cousin at the weekend."
"Don’t worry, I ’ll carry that for you."

mistakes.x: The plane will arrive at 6 — it’s the timetable.
mistakes.v: The plane arrives at 6. (timetable → present simple)

mistakes.x: I think I’m passing the exam.
mistakes.v: I think I’ll pass. (prediction → will)

quiz.q: Look at that car! It ___ crash.
quiz.e: Prediction from evidence → is going to crash.

quiz.q: The train ___ at 10:30.
I ___ Tom for coffee at four. (arrangement)
(phone rings) I ___ get it.
It ___ rain later, but I'm not sure.
We ___ visit Spain next summer. (plan)
The match ___ at 8 pm tonight.

I'm cold. — I ___ close the window.
Choose the evidence-based prediction.
o: She will have a baby — look!
She's going to have a baby — look!
She might to have a baby.

quiz.q: Find the mistake: 'The plane will arrive at 6, it's the timetable.'
Complete: 'We ___ (plan) move house, and I think it ___ (prediction) be stressful.'
o: are going to / are going to

quiz.q: Which shows a possibility?
Complete: 'Hurry! The film ___ at eight and we ___ Jack there.'
Choose the natural arrangement sentence.
o: I have dinner with them tonight.
I'm having dinner with them tonight.
I will have dinner with them, it's arranged.
I might have dinner tonight, it's arranged.

grammar.title: Second conditional
grammar.lead: The second conditional talks about imaginary, unlikely or unreal present and future situations. It uses the past simple in the if-clause and ‘would’ in the result clause.

leadTr.uz: Ikkinchi shart gapi xayoliy yoki ehtimoli past hozirgi/kelajak vaziyatlar uchun: If + past simple, natijada 'would'. If I had time, I would travel.
leadTr.ru: Второй кондиционал — для воображаемых или маловероятных ситуаций: if + past simple, в результате — would. If I had time, I would travel.

grammar.situation: “If I won the lottery, I ’d travel the world.” — The situation is imaginary and unlikely, so we use the past simple + would, not present + will.

blocks.h: Form: if + past simple, would + base
p: The past tense here doesn’t mean past time — it shows the situation is hypothetical.
ex: If I had more money, I would travel.

p: With ‘be’, we often use were for all persons, especially in advice with ‘If I were you’.
ex: If I were you, I’d apologise. · If she were here, she’d help.

p: Use could (ability/possibility) or might (possible result) instead of ‘would’.
ex: If I had a car, I could drive you. · We might win if we tried.

p: First conditional = real/likely; second conditional = unlikely/unreal.
ex: If it rains, I’ll stay in. (likely) · If it snowed in July, I’d be shocked. (unreal)

grammar.tip: For advice, ‘If I were you, I’d…’ is the natural phrase. Don’t mix forms: ‘If I would have money’ is wrong → ‘If I had money, I would…’.
examples: "If I won the lottery, I would buy a house."
"If I were you, I ’d see a doctor."
"She would travel more if she had time."
"If we lived by the sea, we could swim every day."
"What would you do if you lost your job?"
"If he spoke French, he might get the job."

mistakes.x: If I would have money, I would travel.
mistakes.v: If I had money, I would travel. (no “would” after if)

mistakes.x: If I was you, I will help.
mistakes.v: If I were you, I ’d help.

quiz.q: If I ___ rich, I would buy a yacht.
If I had time, I ___ help you.
If I ___ you, I'd apologise.
She would travel if she ___ more money.
If we lived nearer, we ___ visit more often.
What ___ you do if you won a million?
If he ___ harder, he'd pass.
I ___ buy it if it weren't so expensive.
If I had a car, I ___ drive you home.
Choose the unreal situation.
o: If it rains, I'll stay in.
If it snowed in summer, I'd be amazed.

If you heat ice, it melts.

quiz.q: Find the mistake: 'If I would have money, I would travel.'
quiz.e: No ‘would’ in the if-clause: If I had money…

quiz.q: Complete: 'If she ___ here, she ___ what to do.'
Which is correct?
o: If I was you, I will help.
If I were you, I would help.
If I am you, I would help.
If I were you, I will help.
quiz.e: If I were you, I would help.

quiz.q: Complete: 'We ___ win the match if we ___ as a team.'
Choose the natural advice.
o: If I were you, I'd take the job.
If I am you, I take the job.
If I would be you, I take the job.
If I was you, I'll take the job.
quiz.e: If I were you, I’d take the job.

grammar.title: Modals of deduction (present)
grammar.lead: We use modal verbs to say how certain we are about a present situation. ‘Must’ shows we are almost sure something is true; ‘can’t’ that it is impossible; ‘might/may/could’ that it is possible.

leadTr.uz: Hozirgi vaziyat haqidagi taxminlarda modal fe'llar ishonch darajasini ko'rsatadi: 'must' — deyarli aniq, 'can't' — bo'lishi mumkin emas, 'might' — balki.
leadTr.ru: В догадках о настоящем модальные глаголы показывают степень уверенности: must — почти наверняка, can't — невозможно, might — возможно.

p: Use must + base verb when you are sure something is true based on evidence.
ex: The light’s on — she must be home.

p: Use can’t (not ‘mustn’t’) when you are sure something is not true.
ex: He can’t be hungry; he’s just eaten.

p: Use these for things that are possible but uncertain.
ex: She might be at work. · They could be lost.

p: Use modal + be + -ing for an action happening now.
ex: He’s not answering — he must be sleeping.

grammar.tip: The opposite of ‘must be’ (sure it is) is ‘can’t be’ (sure it isn’t), not ‘mustn’t be’. ‘Mustn’t’ means prohibition, not deduction.
examples: "You’ve worked all day — you must be tired."
"That can’t be John; he’s in Spain."
"She might know the answer."
"They must be having dinner; the lights are on."
"It could be true, but I’m not sure."
"He can’t be serious!"

mistakes.x: He isn’t home — he mustn’t be at work.
mistakes.v: …he must be at work. (mustn’t ≠ deduction)
She must be working late. (modal + be + -ing)

quiz.q: The lights are on, so she ___ be home.
He's just eaten, so he ___ be hungry.
quiz.e: Sure it’s not true → can’t be.

quiz.q: I'm not sure, but she ___ be at work.
That ___ be true — it's impossible!
They aren't answering. They ___ be out.
He's wearing a coat, so it ___ be cold.
She speaks five languages — she ___ be clever.
The phone is off. He ___ be sleeping.
This ___ be the right address; the numbers don't match.
Choose the 'possible' modal.
Find the mistake: 'He's not at home, he mustn't be at work.'
quiz.e: For a likely explanation use ‘must be at work’ (mustn’t is prohibition).

quiz.q: Complete: 'She ___ be ill — she ___ be at the gym; her bag is here.'
quiz.e: ‘might be ill’ (possible) + ‘can’t be at the gym’ (impossible — bag is here).

quiz.q: Which is correct?
Complete: 'No one's answering. They ___ out, or they ___ be sleeping.'
quiz.e: Both uncertain → might be / might be.

quiz.q: Choose the present-continuous deduction.

grammar.title: The passive
grammar.lead: We use the passive when the action is more important than the person who does it, or when we don’t know who did it. The object of the active sentence becomes the subject of the passive.

leadTr.uz: Majhul nisbat (passive) harakat bajaruvchidan muhimroq bo'lganda ishlatiladi: The bridge was built in 1905. Faol gapning to'ldiruvchisi egaga aylanadi.
leadTr.ru: Пассив используется, когда действие важнее исполнителя: The bridge was built in 1905. Дополнение активного предложения становится подлежащим.

grammar.situation: “This bridge was built in 1890.” — We use the passive when the action matters more than who did it (or we don’t know who did it).

p: Use the right tense of be + the past participle. Present: am/is/are + pp. Past: was/were + pp.
ex: English is spoken here. · The window was broken yesterday.

p: Use by to say who or what does the action, but only when it is important.
ex: The book was written by Orwell. · He was bitten by a dog.

p: Use it when the doer is unknown, obvious or unimportant, or in formal/scientific writing.
ex: My car was stolen. (we don’t know who) · The results were analysed.

p: Present perfect: has/have been + pp. Future: will be + pp. Modal: can/must be + pp.
ex: The job has been done. · It will be finished soon. · It must be paid today.

grammar.tip: Only verbs with an object (transitive) can be made passive. ‘happen’, ‘arrive’ and ‘sleep’ have no object, so they cannot be passive.
examples: "Millions of phones are made in China."
"The bridge was built in 1890."
"This letter was written by my grandmother."
"The thieves were caught by the police."
"Dinner is being prepared now."
"The work will be finished tomorrow."

mistakes.x: The letter was wrote by John.
mistakes.v: The letter was written by John. (past participle)
The accident happened. (“happen” has no object → no passive)

quiz.q: English ___ in many countries.
The window ___ yesterday.
The passive of 'They make cars here' is 'Cars ___ here.'
This book ___ by Dickens.
The rooms ___ every day.
My bike ___ last week.
Choose the agent: 'The house was designed ___ a famous architect.'
The present perfect passive of 'do' is 'It ___.'
quiz.e: has/have been + pp: has been done.

quiz.q: Which verb CANNOT be passive?
The future passive of 'finish' is 'It ___ tomorrow.'
quiz.e: will be + pp: will be finished.

quiz.q: Find the mistake: 'The letter was wrote by John.'
Make passive: 'Somebody has cleaned the room.'
quiz.e: Present perfect passive: has been cleaned.

quiz.q: Which sentence is correct?
o: The thief was caught by police.
The thief was catch by police.
The thief is catch by police.

quiz.q: Complete (modal passive): 'These forms ___ in pen.'
quiz.e: modal + be + pp: must be completed.

quiz.q: Make passive: 'They are building a new school.'
o: A new school is being built.
quiz.e: Present continuous passive: is being built.

grammar.title: Reported speech: statements
grammar.lead: Reported (indirect) speech tells what someone said without using their exact words. Tenses usually move one step back, and pronouns and time words often change.

leadTr.uz: Ko'chirma gap (reported speech) birovning so'zini aynan keltirmasdan yetkazadi. Zamonlar odatda bir qadam orqaga suriladi, olmosh va vaqt so'zlari o'zgaradi.
leadTr.ru: Косвенная речь передаёт слова без цитирования. Времена обычно сдвигаются на шаг назад, местоимения и слова времени меняются.

p: Move the tense back one step: present simple → past simple; present continuous → past continuous; will → would; can → could.
ex: “I am tired.” → He said he was tired.
“I will call.” → She said she would call.

p: Use tell + a person; use say without a person (or with ‘to’).
ex: She told me she was busy. · She said she was busy.

p: Change pronouns to fit the new speaker, and words like today→that day, tomorrow→the next day, now→then.
ex: “I’ll see you tomorrow.” → He said he’d see me the next day.

p: You can include or leave out that after say/tell.
ex: She said (that) she liked it.

grammar.tip: After tell you must name the listener (tell me/him/us); after say you don’t. ‘He said me’ is wrong → ‘He told me’ or ‘He said’.
examples: "“I’m hungry.” → She said she was hungry."
"“We live in Leeds.” → They said they lived in Leeds."
"“I’ll help you.” → He said he would help me."
"“I can swim.” → She told me she could swim."
"“I’m working now.” → He said he was working then."
"“I bought a car.” → She said she had bought a car."

mistakes.x: He said me that he was late.
mistakes.v: He told me… / He said (that)… (tell + person, say + no person)
She said she would come. (will → would)

quiz.q: "I am tired." → He said he ___ tired.
"I will call." → She said she ___ call.
"I live here." → He said he ___ there.
Choose the correct verb: 'She ___ me she was busy.'
"I can swim." → He said he ___ swim.
"We are eating." → They said they ___ eating.
quiz.e: present continuous → past continuous: were eating.

quiz.q: "I bought a car." → She said she ___ a car.
Choose say/tell: 'He ___ that he was sorry.'
"I'll see you tomorrow." → He said he'd see me ___.
"I don't like it." → She said she ___ it.
Find the mistake: 'He said me that he was late.'
Report: "I have finished my homework."
o: She said she finished her homework.
She said she had finished her homework.
She said she has finished her homework.
She said she finishes her homework.
quiz.e: present perfect → past perfect: had finished.

quiz.q: Which is correct?
o: He told me he was tired.
He said me he was tired.
He say me he was tired.

quiz.q: Report: "We are leaving now."
o: They said they are leaving now.
They said they were leaving then.
They said they will leave now.
quiz.e: present continuous → past continuous; now → then.

quiz.q: Report: "I can't come tomorrow."
o: He said he can't come tomorrow.
He said he couldn't come the next day.
He said he couldn't come tomorrow.
quiz.e: can’t → couldn’t; tomorrow → the next day.

grammar.title: Reported questions & commands
grammar.lead: When we report questions and orders, the structure changes. Reported questions use statement word order, and reported commands use ‘to’ + verb.

leadTr.uz: Savol va buyruqlarni ko'chirishda tuzilish o'zgaradi: ko'chirilgan savolda darak gap tartibi, buyruqda esa 'to' + fe'l ishlatiladi.
leadTr.ru: При передаче вопросов и приказов структура меняется: в косвенном вопросе — прямой порядок слов, в приказе — to + глагол.

p: Keep the question word, then use statement order (subject + verb) with no auxiliary do/does/did.
ex: “Where do you live?” → She asked where I lived.

p: Use if or whether, then statement order.
ex: “Are you ready?” → He asked if I was ready.

p: Use told/asked + person + to + verb. For negatives, use not to.
ex: “Sit down.” → She told me to sit down. · “Don’t move.” → He told me not to move.

p: Reported questions are statements, so they don’t end with a question mark.
ex: He asked where the station was.

grammar.tip: In reported questions, don’t keep the question word order or ‘do/did’: ‘She asked where did I live’ is wrong → ‘She asked where I lived.’
examples: "“What time is it?” → He asked what time it was."
"“Do you like tea?” → She asked if I liked tea."
"“Where are you going?” → He asked where I was going."
"“Close the door.” → She told me to close the door."
"“Please help me.” → He asked me to help him."
"“Don’t be late.” → She told me not to be late."

mistakes.x: She asked me what time was it.
mistakes.v: She asked what time it was. (statement word order)

mistakes.x: He told me to don’t go.
mistakes.v: He told me not to go.

quiz.q: "Where do you live?" → She asked where I ___.
quiz.e: Statement order, backshift: where I lived.

quiz.q: "Are you ready?" → He asked ___ I was ready.
"Sit down." → She told me ___ down.
"Don't run." → He told me ___ run.
"What is your name?" → She asked what my name ___.
"Do you like coffee?" → He asked if I ___ coffee.
"Open the window." → She asked me ___ the window.
"Where are you going?" → He asked where I ___.
quiz.e: present cont. → past cont.: was going.

quiz.q: "Can you swim?" → She asked if I ___ swim.
Choose the correct word order.
o: He asked where did I live.
He asked did where I live.

quiz.q: Find the mistake: 'She asked me what time was it.'
quiz.e: Statement order: what time it was.

quiz.q: Report: "Please don't tell anyone."
o: He asked me not to tell anyone.
He asked me to don't tell anyone.
He asked me don't tell anyone.
He told to not tell anyone.
quiz.e: Negative request → asked me not to tell.

quiz.q: Report: "Have you finished?"
o: She asked if I had finished.
She asked if I have finished.
She asked if had I finished.
quiz.e: Yes/No + present perfect → if I had finished.

quiz.q: Report: "Why are you late?"
o: He asked why was I late.
He asked why I was late.
He asked why I am late.
He asked me why late I was.
quiz.e: Statement order, backshift: why I was late.

quiz.q: Report: "Wait here."
o: She told me to wait there.
She told me to wait here now.
She said me to wait there.

grammar.title: Relative clauses (defining & non-defining)
grammar.lead: Relative clauses add information about a noun. Defining clauses give essential information; non-defining clauses give extra information and are separated by commas.

leadTr.uz: Aniqlovchi (defining) nisbiy gap zaruriy ma'lumot beradi; izohlovchi (non-defining) esa qo'shimcha ma'lumot bo'lib, vergul bilan ajratiladi.
leadTr.ru: Определительные придаточные дают необходимую информацию; распространительные — дополнительную и выделяются запятыми.

p: Give essential information (you need it to know which person or thing). Use who, which, that, where, whose. No commas.
ex: The man who lives next door is a doctor.

p: Give extra, non-essential information, set off by commas. Don’t use ‘that’; don’t omit the pronoun.
ex: My brother, who lives in Leeds, is a teacher.

p: In defining clauses, you can omit who/which/that when it is the object.
ex: The book (that) I read was great.

p: whose shows possession; where refers to a place.
ex: She’s the woman whose car was stolen. · That’s the town where I grew up.

grammar.tip: Use commas only for extra information (non-defining). With commas, never use ‘that’ and never drop the pronoun. Without commas (defining), you can use ‘that’ and may drop an object pronoun.
examples: "The keys that were on the table have gone."
"Paris, which is the capital of France, is beautiful."
"The film (that) we saw was boring."
"My uncle, who is a pilot, travels a lot."
"That’s the house where I was born."
"He’s the boy whose dog bit me."

mistakes.x: My car, that is red, is fast.
mistakes.v: My car, which is red, is fast. (non-defining → which)
The man who called… (people → who)

quiz.q: The woman ___ teaches us is very kind.
I bought a phone ___ takes great photos.
That's the café ___ we first met.
She's the girl ___ brother is famous.
Which clause has extra information (needs commas)?
o: The man who called is here.
My dad, who is 60, still works.

quiz.q: In which sentence can we omit the pronoun?
quiz.e: Object pronoun in a defining clause can be dropped: the book I read.

quiz.q: Non-defining: 'London, ___ is the capital, is huge.'
The keys ___ were on the table are gone.
My sister, ___ lives in Bristol, is a nurse.
Choose the defining clause.
o: The man who called is my boss.
Paris, which I love, is busy.
Tom, whose car broke, is late.

quiz.q: Find the mistake: 'My car, that is red, is fast.'
Complete: 'The hotel ___ we stayed, ___ was by the sea, was lovely.'
quiz.e: Place ‘where we stayed’ + non-defining ‘which was by the sea’.

quiz.q: Which sentence omits the pronoun correctly?
o: The film we saw was good.
The man lives here is nice.
The city is big I visited.
quiz.e: Object pronoun dropped: the film (that) we saw.

quiz.q: Complete: 'He's the player ___ goal won the match, ___ made him famous.'
Choose the correct non-defining sentence.
o: My teacher who is French is kind.
My teacher, who is French, is kind.
My teacher, that is French, is kind.
My teacher which is French is kind.

grammar.title: Past habits: used to & would
grammar.lead: To describe the past we can use ‘used to’ and ‘would’ for repeated habits, but only ‘used to’ works for past states. Both contrast the past with the present.

leadTr.uz: O'tmishdagi takrorlangan odatlar uchun 'used to' ham, 'would' ham bo'ladi, lekin o'tmishdagi HOLATLAR uchun faqat 'used to' ishlaydi: I used to live in Samarkand.
leadTr.ru: Для повторявшихся привычек подходят и used to, и would, но для прошлых СОСТОЯНИЙ — только used to: I used to live in Samarkand.

p: used to + base verb describes past habits and past states that are no longer true.
ex: I used to play tennis. · She used to have long hair.

p: would + base verb describes repeated past actions, but not states. It is common in stories.
ex: Every summer we would visit my grandparents.

blocks.h: would vs. used to with states
p: Don’t use ‘would’ with state verbs (be, have, like, know). Use ‘used to’.
ex: ✓ I used to be shy. · ✗ I would be shy.

p: For ‘used to’: didn’t use to / Did … use to? (no -d).
ex: He didn’t use to like coffee. · Did you use to live here?

grammar.tip: Use ‘would’ only for repeated actions. For past states (be, have, like, know), you must use ‘used to’: ‘I used to have a bike’, not ‘I would have a bike’.
examples: "We used to live by the sea."
"On Sundays, my dad would cook a big breakfast."
"She used to be very shy."
"He didn’t use to exercise, but now he runs daily."
"As children, we would play outside all day."
"Did you use to have a dog?"

mistakes.x: I would have a red car when I was young.
mistakes.v: I used to have a red car. (state → used to)

mistakes.x: Did you used to live here?
mistakes.v: Did you use to live here? (after did → no -d)

quiz.q: I ___ play football every day as a child.
Every winter, we ___ go skiing.
She ___ have long hair.
They ___ visit us every summer.
He ___ be very thin.
Which sentence is WRONG?
quiz.e: ‘would’ can’t be used with the state ‘be’.

quiz.q: Negative: 'I ___ like vegetables.'
On holiday, we ___ swim in the sea every morning.
___ you use to have a bike?
Choose the state-verb sentence (only 'used to').
o: I used to have a cat.
quiz.e: ‘have’ is a state → used to have.

quiz.q: Find the mistake: 'I would have a red car when I was young.'
Complete: 'My grandmother ___ tell us stories, and she ___ a wonderful voice.'
quiz.e: Repeated action ‘would tell’ + state ‘used to have’.

quiz.q: Which is correct for a past habit and a past state?
o: I would be a teacher and would smoke.
I used to be a teacher and would smoke.
I would be a teacher and used to smoke.
I use to be a teacher and would smoke.
quiz.e: State ‘used to be’ + repeated action ‘would smoke’.

quiz.q: Complete: '___ they ___ live in the countryside?'
quiz.e: Did + use to: Did they use to live…?

quiz.q: Choose the natural sentence.
o: When I was a kid, I would have a dog.
When I was a kid, I used to have a dog.
When I was a kid, I use to have a dog.
When I was a kid, I am used to have a dog.

grammar.title: Gerunds & infinitives
grammar.lead: Many verbs are followed by a gerund (-ing) and others by an infinitive (to + verb). Some verbs take either form, and a few change meaning depending on which you choose.

leadTr.uz: Ko'p fe'llardan keyin gerund (-ing), boshqalaridan keyin infinitiv keladi. Ba'zilari ikkala shaklni oladi, ayrimlarida esa ma'no o'zgaradi: stop doing / stop to do.
leadTr.ru: После многих глаголов идёт герундий, после других — инфинитив. Некоторые принимают обе формы, а у части меняется смысл: stop doing / stop to do.

p: After enjoy, finish, avoid, suggest, mind, keep, practise, can’t stand, look forward to, and after prepositions, use the -ing form.
ex: I enjoy cooking. · She’s good at drawing. · I look forward to seeing you.

p: After want, decide, hope, plan, promise, agree, offer, refuse, manage, learn, would like, use to + verb.
ex: We decided to leave. · He refused to help.

p: Some verbs take an object then to-infinitive: want, ask, tell, allow, advise, expect.
ex: She asked me to wait. · They allowed us to stay.

p: A few verbs change meaning: stop, remember, try, forget.
ex: I stopped smoking. (gave it up) · I stopped to smoke. (paused in order to)

grammar.tip: After prepositions (about, of, at, in, before, after, without), always use the -ing form: ‘I’m interested in learning’, ‘before going out’.
examples: "I can’t stand waiting in queues."
"She decided to study abroad."
"He’s thinking about changing jobs."
"They asked me to help them."
"Remember to lock the door. (don’t forget)"
"I’ll never forget visiting Rome. (the memory)"

mistakes.x: I’m interested in to learn Spanish.
mistakes.v: I’m interested in learning Spanish. (preposition + -ing)
They allowed us to stay.

quiz.q: I enjoy ___ to music.
We decided ___ early.
She's good at ___.
He refused ___ the question.
Do you mind ___ the window?
They asked me ___ them.
I'm thinking about ___ a new car.
She managed ___ the problem.
We're looking forward to ___ you.
He suggested ___ a taxi.
Find the mistake: 'I'm interested in to learn Spanish.'
Choose the correct meaning: 'He stopped to smoke' means ___.
o: he paused in order to smoke
quiz.e: stop + to = pause in order to do something.

quiz.q: Complete: 'Please remember ___ the door, and I'll never forget ___ here as a child.'
Which is correct?
quiz.e: allow + object + to: allowed us to stay.

quiz.q: Complete: 'I tried ___ the box, but it was locked, so I tried ___ a knife.'
quiz.e: try to do (attempt) + try doing (experiment): to open / using.

grammar.title: Comparing: as…as, less, modifiers
grammar.lead: Beyond basic comparatives, we can show that two things are equal, that one is inferior, or how big the difference is. These patterns make comparisons more precise.

leadTr.uz: Oddiy qiyoslashdan tashqari tenglikni (as…as), kamlikni (less) va farq hajmini (much bigger, a bit smaller) ifodalash mumkin — bu qiyoslashni aniqroq qiladi.
leadTr.ru: Помимо простого сравнения можно выразить равенство (as…as), меньшую степень (less) и размер разницы (much bigger, a bit smaller).

p: Use as + adjective + as to say two things are the same, and not as … as for inequality.
ex: She’s as tall as her brother. · It’s not as cold as yesterday.

p: Use less + adjective + than (the opposite of ‘more … than’), usually with longer adjectives.
ex: This film is less interesting than the book.

p: Make comparatives stronger or weaker with much, far, a lot, a bit, slightly.
ex: He’s much taller than me. · It’s a bit warmer today.

p: Use ‘the + comparative … the + comparative’ to show that two things change together.
ex: The more you practise, the better you get.

grammar.tip: To strengthen a comparative, use much or far (much/far better), not ‘very’. ‘Very better’ is wrong; ‘much better’ is correct.
examples: "Maths is as difficult as physics for me."
"This phone is not as expensive as that one."
"Today is far hotter than yesterday."
"The book is less exciting than the film."
"He runs a bit faster than me."
"The harder you work, the more you earn."

mistakes.x: This car is very better than mine.
mistakes.v: …is much better than mine. (much/far, not very)

mistakes.x: She is as tall than him.
mistakes.v: She is as tall as him.

quiz.q: She is ___ tall ___ her sister.
It isn't ___ cold ___ yesterday.
This book is ___ interesting than that one.
He's ___ taller than me.
Today is ___ a bit warmer than yesterday.
quiz.e: ‘just a bit warmer’ — slightly (just/a bit) modifies the comparative.

quiz.q: My phone is ___ expensive ___ yours.
The film was ___ exciting than the book.
He's ___ better at chess than I am.
Complete: '___ you practise, ___ you become.'
Choose the equality sentence.
o: She is as tall as him.
She is more tall than him.

quiz.q: Find the mistake: 'This car is very better than mine.'
Complete: 'It's ___ as difficult ___ I expected — much easier, in fact.'
Which means 'they are equal'?
o: A is less good than B.
A is much better than B.
A is as good as B.
A isn't as good as B.

quiz.q: Complete: 'The ___ we leave, the ___ we'll arrive.'
Choose the correctly modified comparative.

grammar.title: Quantifiers
grammar.lead: Quantifiers tell us about amount and number. At B1 we extend beyond some/any to all, most, both, neither, none, each and every, and learn how they combine with nouns and ‘of’.

leadTr.uz: B1 darajasida some/any dan tashqari all, most, both, neither, none, each va every so'zlarini hamda ularning ot bilan qanday birikishini o'rganamiz.
leadTr.ru: На B1 мы выходим за пределы some/any: all, most, both, neither, none, each, every и их сочетания с существительными.

p: Use these for general amounts. With ‘the/my/these’ + noun, add of: most of the students.
ex: Most people like music. · None of the answers were right.

p: both = the two together; neither = not one and not the other; either = one or the other.
ex: Both films are good. · Neither answer is correct. · Either day is fine.

p: Both mean ‘all, seen individually’, and take a singular verb. ‘every’ for the whole group; ‘each’ for the individuals.
ex: Every student has a book. · Each answer is different.

p: a few + countable, a little + uncountable, several = more than a few (countable).
ex: A few people came. · A little milk. · Several students passed.

grammar.tip: every and each are followed by a singular noun and verb: ‘Every student is here’, not ‘every students are here’.
examples: "Most of my friends live abroad."
"None of the shops were open."
"Both answers are correct."
"Neither of us wants to go."
"Every child needs love."
"Several people complained."

mistakes.v: Every student is present. (every + singular)
Most people are kind. (no “of” without the/my)

quiz.q: ___ people enjoy music.
___ of the students passed.
___ answers are correct — well done!
___ student has a textbook.
I have ___ money, just a little.
___ of the answers was right; they were all wrong.
___ of us wants to leave; we're both happy.
quiz.e: Not one and not the other → Neither.

quiz.q: ___ child in the class is different.
___ students complained about the test.
quiz.e: More than a few, countable → Several.

quiz.q: Choose the correct verb: 'Every student ___ here.'
Find the mistake: 'Every students are present.'
quiz.e: every + singular: Every student is present.

quiz.q: Complete: '___ of the two options is fine; choose ___ you like.'
quiz.e: Either of the two is fine; choose either.

quiz.q: Which is correct?
quiz.e: General statement → Most people (no ‘of’ without the/my/these).

quiz.q: Complete: '___ of my friends came, but ___ stayed late.'
quiz.e: All of my friends came, but none stayed late.

quiz.q: Choose the sentence with correct agreement.
o: Each of the rooms have a bed.
Each of the rooms has a bed.
Each of the room have a bed.

grammar.title: Conditionals: zero, first & linkers
grammar.lead: Conditionals describe results that follow from conditions. The zero conditional states facts; the first conditional describes likely future situations. Linkers like unless and as long as add precision.

leadTr.uz: Shart gaplar natija va shartni bog'laydi: zero conditional — faktlar, first conditional — ehtimoliy kelajak. Unless, as long as, in case kabi bog'lovchilar ma'noni boyitadi.
leadTr.ru: Кондиционалы связывают условие и результат: zero — факты, first — вероятное будущее. Unless, as long as, in case обогащают смысл.

p: Use if/when + present, present for things that are always true.
ex: If you heat water, it boils.

p: Use if + present, will + base for real, likely future situations.
ex: If it rains, we’ll stay in.

p: unless = if … not. It introduces the only condition that changes the result.
ex: I won’t go unless you come too. (= if you don’t come)

blocks.h: as long as / provided that / in case
p: as long as / provided that = on condition that; in case = as a precaution.
ex: You can stay as long as you’re quiet. · Take an umbrella in case it rains.

grammar.tip: Don’t use ‘will’ after if/unless/as long as/in case in the condition: ‘If it will rain’ is wrong → ‘If it rains, we’ll stay in.’
examples: "If you mix blue and yellow, you get green."
"If you study, you’ll pass."
"We’ll be late unless we hurry."
"You can borrow it as long as you return it."
"I’ll take my phone in case you call."
"Provided that you pay, you can join."

grammar.title: Articles: a / an / the / zero
grammar.lead: Articles are small but tricky. ‘A/an’ introduces something new or one of many; ‘the’ points to something specific or already known; and we use no article (zero) for general ideas and most plurals/uncountables.

leadTr.uz: Artikllar kichik, lekin murakkab: 'a/an' — yangi yoki noaniq narsa, 'the' — aniq yoki ma'lum narsa, ba'zi hollarda esa artikl umuman ishlatilmaydi.
leadTr.ru: Артикли малы, но коварны: a/an — новое или неопределённое, the — конкретное или известное, а иногда артикль не нужен вовсе.

p: Use a/an with singular countable nouns mentioned for the first time or as examples. ‘an’ before a vowel sound.
ex: I saw a dog. · She’s an engineer. · It takes an hour. (silent h)

p: Use the when both speaker and listener know which one, for unique things, and when mentioned again.
ex: The sun is hot. · I bought a book; the book was great.

p: Use no article for plural and uncountable nouns in general, and most names, meals, and many places.
ex: Dogs are loyal. · I like music. · We have lunch at one.

p: Some places take ‘the’ or zero by convention.
ex: go to school/work/bed (zero) · play the piano · in the morning

grammar.tip: Use ‘a/an’ when it’s new or one of many, and ‘the’ when it’s specific or already known. For general statements with plurals/uncountables, use no article: ‘Books are useful’, not ‘The books are useful’.
examples: "She’s a teacher and an artist."
"The Earth goes round the Sun."
"I love coffee in the morning."
"We went to school by bus."
"He plays the guitar very well."
"Children need plenty of sleep."

reading.title: A Change of Career
reading.text:
For ten years, Daniel had worked as an accountant in a busy office in Birmingham. The salary was good, but he had never really enjoyed the job. He often felt bored, and by the end of each week he was exhausted.
Last year, everything changed. While he was helping a friend repair an old house, he realised how much he loved working with his hands. After a few months, he made a brave decision: he resigned from his job and started training as a carpenter.
Now Daniel earns less money than before, but he is much happier. He says he should have changed careers years ago. 'If I had known how good it would feel,' he says, 'I would have done it sooner.'
