reading.title: The Remote Working Debate
reading.text:
Since the pandemic, working from home has become normal for millions of people. Supporters argue that it offers a better work-life balance: employees save hours that would otherwise be wasted commuting, and many report feeling less stressed and more productive.
Not everyone is convinced, however. Some managers worry that staff who work remotely are harder to supervise and less connected to their colleagues. Younger workers, in particular, may miss the informal learning that happens in an office, where they can pick up skills simply by watching experienced people.
The truth probably lies somewhere in between. A growing number of companies in Manchester and London now offer a 'hybrid' model, in which employees spend part of the week at home and part in the office. Had this option been available ten years ago, it might have seemed strange. Today, it is increasingly seen as the best of both worlds.

quiz.q: What is one advantage of remote work mentioned?
quiz.e: It offers a better work-life balance.

quiz.q: Why do some managers worry?
quiz.e: Remote staff are harder to supervise and less connected.

quiz.q: What might younger workers miss?
quiz.e: They may miss informal learning from experienced colleagues.

quiz.q: What is the 'hybrid' model?
quiz.e: Part of the week at home, part in the office.

quiz.q: What is the writer's overall view of hybrid work?
o: It is the best of both worlds.
quiz.e: It is increasingly seen as the best of both worlds.

reading.title: Living with Artificial Intelligence
reading.text:
Artificial intelligence is no longer science fiction. It already recommends the films we watch, filters our emails, and helps doctors read medical scans. For many, these developments are exciting; for others, they are a cause for concern.
Those who welcome AI point to its potential to save lives and time. A computer can examine thousands of images far faster than a human, spotting patterns that might otherwise be missed. In industries from farming to finance, AI is helping people make better decisions.
Yet the same technology raises difficult questions. If a self-driving car causes an accident, who is responsible? As machines take over more tasks, some jobs will certainly disappear. Supporters argue that new jobs will be created, just as they were during the Industrial Revolution. Critics are less sure. What seems clear is that AI is here to stay, and societies will need to decide carefully how to use it.

quiz.q: What does the text say AI already does?
quiz.e: It recommends films, filters emails and helps read scans.

quiz.q: Why is AI useful in medicine?
o: It examines images faster than humans.
quiz.e: It can examine many images quickly and spot patterns.

quiz.q: What difficult question does the text raise?
o: who is responsible for a self-driving car accident
quiz.e: Responsibility for a self-driving car accident.

quiz.q: What do supporters say about jobs?
quiz.e: They argue new jobs will be created.

quiz.q: What conclusion does the writer reach?
o: AI is here to stay and must be used carefully.
quiz.e: AI is here to stay; societies must decide how to use it.

reading.title: Why We Put Things Off
reading.text:
Almost everyone procrastinates. We delay important tasks, choosing instead to check our phones, tidy a drawer, or make yet another cup of tea. We know we are wasting time, and yet we do it anyway. Why?
Psychologists suggest that procrastination is not really about laziness. It is more often about emotion. When a task makes us feel anxious or bored, our brain looks for an escape, and a quick, pleasant distraction provides instant relief. The problem, of course, is that the relief never lasts, and the task only grows more stressful.
The good news is that procrastination can be managed. Experts recommend breaking a large task into small steps, so that it feels less frightening. It also helps to forgive yourself for past delays; research has shown that students who stopped criticising themselves actually procrastinated less in future. In other words, being kinder to ourselves may be the first step towards getting things done.

quiz.q: According to psychologists, procrastination is mainly about ___.
quiz.e: It is more about emotion than laziness.

quiz.q: Why does the brain seek distraction?
o: for instant relief from anxiety or boredom
quiz.e: Distraction gives instant relief from bad feelings.

quiz.q: What is the problem with distraction?
quiz.e: The relief never lasts and the task grows more stressful.

quiz.q: What do experts recommend for big tasks?
quiz.e: Break a large task into small steps.

quiz.q: What did research on students show?
quiz.e: Students who stopped self-criticism procrastinated less.

reading.title: Report: Improving the Town Library
reading.text:
Introduction
The purpose of this report is to assess the current state of Brighton Central Library and to recommend improvements. The findings are based on a survey of 200 users and interviews with staff.

Findings
The majority of users praised the library's wide selection of books. However, several problems were identified. Firstly, the opening hours were felt to be too limited, particularly for those who work full-time. Secondly, the building's Wi-Fi was described as slow and unreliable. Finally, a number of younger visitors complained that there was nowhere quiet to study.

Recommendations
In light of these findings, it is recommended that the library extend its opening hours into the evening. Furthermore, the Wi-Fi system should be upgraded as a priority. Were a quiet study area to be created on the upper floor, it would almost certainly attract more students.

Conclusion
With relatively modest investment, the library could serve the community far more effectively.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of the report?
o: to assess it and recommend improvements
quiz.e: To assess the library and recommend improvements.

quiz.q: How was the information gathered?
quiz.e: A survey of 200 users and staff interviews.

quiz.q: What did users praise?
Which was NOT a problem identified?
What is recommended for the upper floor?
quiz.e: Creating a quiet study area would attract students.

reading.title: The Cost of Cheap Travel
reading.text:
Never before has travel been so affordable. Budget airlines now offer flights across Europe for the price of a meal, and millions of us take advantage every year. Yet this golden age of cheap travel comes at a price that does not appear on the ticket.
The most obvious cost is environmental. Aviation produces a significant share of carbon emissions, and a single long flight can undo months of careful recycling. Less visible, but no less serious, is the impact on popular destinations. Cities such as Venice and Barcelona have become so crowded with visitors that local residents are being pushed out of their own neighbourhoods.
None of this means we should stop travelling altogether. Travel broadens the mind and supports countless livelihoods. What it does suggest is that we should travel more thoughtfully — flying less often, staying longer, and respecting the places we visit. Only if tourists and governments act together will the benefits of travel be preserved for future generations.

quiz.q: What point does the opening make about travel today?
o: It has never been so affordable.
quiz.e: Travel has never been so affordable.

quiz.q: What is described as the most obvious cost?
What problem do Venice and Barcelona face?
quiz.e: Overcrowding is pushing local residents out.

quiz.q: Does the writer say we should stop travelling?
quiz.e: We should travel more thoughtfully, not stop.

quiz.q: What does the writer say is needed to preserve travel's benefits?
quiz.e: Tourists and governments must act together.

reading.title: Reading set: Ideas & evidence I
reading.text:
Each task below contains its own short passage. Read it closely, then answer — this trains exactly the kind of reading you will meet in real academic texts and exams.

Quyida har bir topshiriqning o'z qisqa matni bor. Diqqat bilan o'qing, so'ng javob bering.

quiz.q:
Passage: Recent archaeological discoveries along the ancient Silk Road reveal that the exchange of goods was accompanied by an equally significant transfer of agricultural knowledge. Crop varieties, farming techniques, and irrigation methods all traveled alongside silk and spices, fundamentally reshaping food production across Eurasia.

Which best states the main idea?
o: The Silk Road facilitated trade in goods AND the spread of agricultural knowledge across Eurasia
Irrigation methods developed in Asia were superior to those used in Europe
Silk Road sites contain artifacts related to farming and food production
The Silk Road was primarily a route for luxury goods between Asia and Europe
quiz.e: The passage argues the Silk Road transferred BOTH goods AND agricultural knowledge. C covers the full argument. A and B are too narrow. D is not stated.

quiz.q:
Passage: The assumption that digital technology has uniformly shortened human attention spans is not supported by evidence. While social media correlates with brief engagement, long-form video streaming and e-reading involve sustained attention comparable to traditional media.

Which best states the central claim?
o: Digital technology has significantly shortened the average human attention span
Long-form streaming requires greater attention than reading physical books
The relationship between digital technology and attention is more complex than a simple decline narrative
Social media platforms are specifically designed to capture user attention
quiz.e: The passage challenges the 'uniformly shortened' assumption — not all digital activities reduce attention. C captures this nuance. A is what the passage contradicts. B and D are too narrow.

quiz.q:
Passage: Biologist E.O. Wilson coined 'biophilia' to describe an innate human affinity for other living systems. He argued that millions of years of evolution hardwired humans to find beauty and meaning in nature — a connection he believed modern urban life systematically erodes.

The text is primarily about
o: Wilson's argument that humans have an evolutionarily rooted connection to nature that urbanization threatens
The psychological effects of city living without access to natural environments
The scientific debate surrounding Wilson's hypothesis
Wilson's career contributions to evolutionary science
quiz.e: The passage presents Wilson's specific argument: humans are hardwired for nature AND urbanization erodes this. B captures both parts. A implies debate (not stated). C and D are too narrow.

quiz.q:
Passage: The narrative that the printing press single-handedly caused the Protestant Reformation oversimplifies history. While Gutenberg's invention accelerated Luther's ideas, religious discontent had been building for over a century before 1517, driven by clerical corruption and economic grievances.

The central claim is that
o: The Reformation was caused primarily by economics rather than religion
The press was one factor in the Reformation, but tensions had deeper roots that preceded it
Gutenberg's press was not invented until after Luther's 95 Theses
Luther's ideas would have spread even without the printing press
quiz.e: The passage argues the press-caused-Reformation narrative is oversimplified because discontent predated print. C captures this. A is factually wrong. B distorts. D is speculative.

reading.title: Reading set: Ideas & evidence II
reading.text:
Each task below contains its own short passage. Read it closely, then answer — this trains exactly the kind of reading you will meet in real academic texts and exams.

Quyida har bir topshiriqning o'z qisqa matni bor. Diqqat bilan o'qing, so'ng javob bering.

quiz.q:
Passage: As Arctic permafrost thaws, it releases stored carbon dioxide and methane, which accelerate warming, which causes more thawing. What makes this alarming is that permafrost contains roughly twice as much carbon as is currently in the atmosphere.

The main idea is
o: Climate change poses threats to Arctic ecosystems that scientists are only beginning to understand
Arctic permafrost stores large quantities of carbon accumulated over thousands of years
The thawing of permafrost creates a self-reinforcing cycle that could dramatically amplify climate change
Scientists have recently discovered that permafrost contains methane in addition to carbon dioxide
quiz.e: The key argument is the feedback loop PLUS the alarming carbon quantity. B captures both. A and C are individual details. D is too vague.

quiz.q:
Passage: Scholar Nancy Armstrong argues that the rise of the Victorian novel was inseparable from the rise of middle-class femininity. The idealized domestic woman depicted in these novels was not merely a reflection of social reality but an active construct that helped produce it — shaping how readers understood desire and virtue.

What is the central claim?
o: Victorian heroines demonstrated virtues that real women were expected to emulate
Victorian novels were primarily written by and for middle-class women
Armstrong argues domestic fiction both reflected and actively shaped Victorian ideals of femininity
Victorian domestic fiction was more concerned with class than gender
quiz.e: Armstrong's argument has two parts: novels were part of the rise of femininity AND they actively produced that femininity. B captures both. A is not stated. C misses 'actively constructed.' D contradicts the text.

quiz.q:
Passage: Traditional economics treats humans as rational actors who maximize self-interest. However, behavioral economics research demonstrates that human decision-making is systematically shaped by cognitive biases, emotional states, and social influences that often lead people to act against their own stated preferences.

The passage primarily argues that
o: Behavioral economics has replaced traditional economics as the dominant framework
Human beings are fundamentally irrational and incapable of sound economic decisions
Cognitive biases can occasionally cause people to deviate from economically rational behavior
Traditional economic models fail to accurately capture how humans actually make decisions
quiz.e: The passage says traditional models assume rationality BUT behavioral economics shows systematic biases. B captures this. A is too strong. C is too extreme. D is too weak — 'occasionally' vs. 'systematically.'

quiz.q:
Passage: Standardized testing was justified by the need for objective measures. Yet critics argue these tests measure a narrow band of skills, create incentives to 'teach to the test,' and systematically disadvantage lower-income students who lack access to test preparation resources.

The main idea is
o: Test preparation resources give wealthier students an unfair advantage
Despite their stated purpose of objective measurement, standardized tests have several significant shortcomings
Standardized testing was introduced to American schools in the 1980s
Academic performance has declined since the adoption of standardized testing
quiz.e: The passage presents the purpose AND multiple criticisms. B captures this full structure. A is background only. C is one specific criticism. D is not stated.

reading.title: Reading set: Author's craft
reading.text:
Each task below contains its own short passage. Read it closely, then answer — this trains exactly the kind of reading you will meet in real academic texts and exams.

Quyida har bir topshiriqning o'z qisqa matni bor. Diqqat bilan o'qing, so'ng javob bering.

quiz.q:
Text: 'The architect's early sketches were rough and provisional, but they captured the essential character of the building she would eventually construct.'

As used in the text, 'provisional' most nearly means
quiz.e: The sketches are 'rough' and not final — they are preliminary. 'Provisional' = temporary, not yet final. 'Legally authorized' and 'provided as a benefit' are other senses of 'provision.'

quiz.q:
Text: 'Anthropologists studying the remote community found that its social structures were remarkably resilient, having persisted through centuries of external disruption and internal conflict.'

As used in the text, 'resilient' most nearly means
o: resistant to all forms of change
able to withstand and recover from difficulties
quiz.e: The structures 'persisted through' disruption — they survived and endured. 'Resilient' = able to withstand and recover. 'Elastic' is a physical sense. 'Resistant to all change' is too absolute.

quiz.q:
Text: 'Though the two theories appear superficially similar, closer examination reveals they rest on fundamentally incompatible assumptions about the nature of consciousness.'

As used in the text, 'incompatible' most nearly means
o: unable to coexist or be reconciled
quiz.e: The assumptions 'cannot coexist' — they can't both be right simultaneously. 'Incompatible' = unable to be reconciled. 'Difficult to understand' changes the meaning entirely.

quiz.q:
Text: 'The documentary draws on extensive archival footage to illuminate aspects of the artist's life that were previously unknown.'

As used in the text, 'illuminate' most nearly means
quiz.e: The footage 'sheds light on' previously unknown aspects — makes them clear and understandable. The physical lighting sense doesn't apply here.

listening.title: A University Lecture
listening.script: Good morning, everyone. Today we're looking at the psychology of decision-making. Now, we like to think we make choices logically, weighing up the facts. But research suggests otherwise. In fact, most of our decisions are driven by emotion and by mental shortcuts the brain uses to save effort. These shortcuts are usually helpful, but they can lead to predictable mistakes. For example, people tend to fear losing something far more than they value gaining the same thing. This is called loss aversion, and we'll explore it in detail after the break. For now, I'd like you to read chapter four before next week's seminar.

quiz.q: What is the lecture about?
quiz.e: It is about the psychology of decision-making.

quiz.q: What does research suggest about our decisions?
o: They are driven by emotion and mental shortcuts.
quiz.e: Most decisions are driven by emotion and shortcuts.

quiz.q: What are the mental shortcuts usually like?
o: usually helpful but sometimes lead to mistakes
quiz.e: Usually helpful, but can cause predictable mistakes.

quiz.q: What is 'loss aversion'?
o: fearing loss more than valuing an equal gain
quiz.e: Fearing loss more than valuing the same gain.

quiz.q: What must students do before the seminar?
quiz.e: Read chapter four before next week's seminar.

listening.title: A Job Interview
listening.script: So, thank you for coming in. Could you tell me why you applied for this marketing role? Of course. I've followed your company for years, and I really admire your creative campaigns. I felt my experience would be a good fit. Tell me about a challenge you've faced. In my last job, we lost a major client unexpectedly. Rather than panic, I led a small team to win back three smaller clients within a month. That's impressive. And where do you see yourself in five years? Honestly, I'd like to be managing my own team here, helping to develop the kind of campaigns that first attracted me to you. Excellent. We'll be in touch by the end of the week.

quiz.q: What role is the candidate applying for?
Why did she apply?
o: she admires the company's creative campaigns
quiz.e: She admires their creative campaigns and felt it fit.

quiz.q: What challenge did she describe?
o: losing a major client and winning back smaller ones
quiz.e: Losing a major client, then winning back three smaller ones.

quiz.q: Where does she see herself in five years?
quiz.e: Managing her own team at the company.

quiz.q: When will she hear back?
o: by the end of the week
quiz.e: By the end of the week.

listening.title: A Discussion on Social Media
listening.script: Welcome back. Today we're debating whether social media does more harm than good. Sarah, you start. Well, I think the benefits are huge. It keeps families connected across the world and gives a voice to people who would otherwise be ignored. But James, you disagree? I do. I'm not denying the benefits, but we can't ignore the harm. Studies link heavy use to anxiety, especially among teenagers. People compare their real lives to others' perfect online images, and they feel worse. Sarah, a response? I'd say the problem isn't the technology itself, but how we use it. With better education, we could enjoy the good and avoid the worst. That's a fair point. We'll take some calls after this.

quiz.q: What is the debate about?
o: whether social media does more harm than good
quiz.e: Whether social media does more harm than good.

quiz.q: What benefit does Sarah mention?
o: it keeps families connected and gives a voice
quiz.e: It connects families and gives people a voice.

quiz.q: What harm does James describe?
o: a link to anxiety, especially in teenagers
quiz.e: Heavy use is linked to anxiety in teenagers.

quiz.q: Why do people feel worse, according to James?
o: they compare their lives to others' perfect images
quiz.e: They compare real lives to perfect online images.

quiz.q: What is Sarah's final point?
o: The problem is how we use it, not the technology.
quiz.e: The problem is how we use it; education could help.

listening.title: A Climate News Report
listening.script: In environmental news, a major report published today warns that global temperatures are rising faster than previously expected. Scientists say that without urgent action, many coastal cities could face serious flooding within decades. However, the report is not entirely negative. It notes that the cost of renewable energy, such as solar and wind power, has fallen dramatically, making clean energy cheaper than coal in much of the world. The authors argue that the technology to solve the crisis already exists; what is missing is political will. A global summit will be held in Leeds next month, where world leaders will be under pressure to agree on stronger targets. Critics, however, fear that promises will once again be broken.

quiz.q: What does the new report warn about?
quiz.e: Global temperatures are rising faster than expected.

quiz.q: What could happen to coastal cities?
quiz.e: They could face serious flooding within decades.

quiz.q: What positive point does the report make?
o: renewable energy has become much cheaper
quiz.e: Renewable energy costs have fallen dramatically.

quiz.q: According to the authors, what is missing?
quiz.e: The technology exists; political will is missing.

quiz.q: What do critics fear about the summit?
quiz.e: They fear promises will once again be broken.

speaking.title: Arguing a position
speaking.prompt: Should social media be regulated? Argue your position for 90 seconds.
tips: State your thesis in one sentence.
Concede one opposing point, then refute it.

tips: Trends: there has been a steady rise in…

tips: Passive voice: it is heated / it gets stored…

grammar.title: Inversion for emphasis
grammar.lead: Advanced English uses inversion — putting the auxiliary before the subject — to add drama and formality. It is common in writing, speeches, and formal speaking.

leadTr.uz: Ilg'or ingliz tilida urg'u berish uchun inversiya ishlatiladi — yordamchi fe'l egadan oldin keladi. Bu yozma nutq va rasmiy uslubda ko'p uchraydi.
leadTr.ru: В продвинутом английском для усиления используется инверсия — вспомогательный глагол ставится перед подлежащим. Это характерно для письменной и формальной речи.

p: After never, rarely, seldom, little, no sooner, not only — invert subject and auxiliary.
ex: Never have I seen such dedication.
Not only did she win, but she also broke the record.

p: Had / Should / Were can replace 'if' in formal conditionals.
ex: Had I known, I would have called.
Should you need anything, ask.

p: So + adjective and Such + noun phrase can open the sentence with inversion.
ex: So intense was the storm that flights stopped.
Such was the noise that nobody slept.

grammar.tip: Inversion is a spice, not a staple — one per paragraph is plenty.
examples: Rarely does a film capture a book so well.
Little did they know what awaited them.
No sooner had we arrived than it started to rain.

mistakes.x: Never I have seen such a thing.
mistakes.v: Never have I seen such a thing — auxiliary before subject.

mistakes.x: Not only she sings, but she dances.
mistakes.v: Not only does she sing, but she also dances.

quiz.q: ___ had the meeting started when the fire alarm rang.
quiz.e: No sooner had X happened than Y — paired with 'than'.

quiz.q: ___ you require assistance, our team is available around the clock.
quiz.e: Should = if, in formal conditionals: Should you require…

quiz.q: Not only ___ the deadline, she exceeded every target.
quiz.e: After 'not only' use auxiliary + subject + verb: did she meet.

quiz.q: ___ was the demand that the servers crashed.
quiz.e: Such + was + noun phrase: Such was the demand that…

quiz.q: Had I known about the traffic, I ___ earlier.
quiz.e: Had I known = If I had known → would have left (third conditional).

grammar.title: Cleft sentences
grammar.lead: Cleft sentences (It was… that…, What I need is…) split one message into two clauses to control emphasis — a hallmark of fluent, natural English.

leadTr.uz: Cleft gaplar (It was… that…, What I need is…) bitta fikrni ikki qismga bo'lib, urg'uni boshqaradi — bu ravon ingliz tilining belgisi.
leadTr.ru: Расщеплённые предложения (It was… that…, What I need is…) делят одну мысль на две части, управляя акцентом — признак свободного владения языком.

p: Emphasise who, what, when or where with It + be + focus + that/who.
ex: It was Maria who solved it.
It was in 2019 that everything changed.

p: What + clause + be + focus emphasises the thing itself.
ex: What I need is a long holiday.
What annoyed me was the silence afterwards.

p: All + clause + be + focus means 'the only thing'.
ex: All I asked for was five minutes.
All it takes is practice.

grammar.tip: In speech, wh-clefts buy you thinking time while sounding sophisticated.
examples: It's the small details that matter.
What makes her different is her patience.
All we can do is wait.

mistakes.x: It was Maria which solved it.
mistakes.v: Use who for people: It was Maria who solved it.

mistakes.x: What I need it is a holiday.
mistakes.v: No extra pronoun: What I need is a holiday.

quiz.q: ___ the ending that ruined the film for me.
What impressed the panel ___ her honesty.
quiz.e: Wh-cleft takes singular be: What impressed them was…

quiz.q: ___ I'm saying is that we need more time.
quiz.e: What I'm saying is… — emphasising the message.

quiz.q: It was only when I reread the letter ___ I understood.
quiz.e: It-cleft closes with that: …that I understood.

grammar.title: The subjunctive & formal structures
grammar.lead: Formal English preserves the subjunctive after verbs like suggest, demand, insist — and fixed phrases like 'be that as it may'. Mastering it lifts your writing register instantly.

leadTr.uz: Rasmiy ingliz tilida suggest, demand, insist kabi fe'llardan keyin subjunktiv saqlanadi. Uni egallash yozuv uslubingizni darhol ko'taradi.
leadTr.ru: Формальный английский сохраняет сослагательное наклонение после глаголов suggest, demand, insist. Владение им сразу повышает регистр письма.

p: After suggest/recommend/demand/insist + that, use the base form for all persons.
ex: They insisted that she be present.
We recommend that he take the earlier train.

p: Some subjunctives survive only in set expressions.
ex: Be that as it may…
Suffice it to say…
Far be it from me to judge.

p: Use 'were' for all persons in hypotheticals.
ex: If I were in your position…
I wish it were simpler.

grammar.tip: In American English the mandative subjunctive is standard; British English often uses 'should' instead — both are correct.
examples: The board demanded that the report be rewritten.
It is essential that every voice be heard.
If he were honest, he'd admit it.

mistakes.x: They suggested that he goes home.
mistakes.v: Base form after suggest: …that he go home.

mistakes.x: If I was you, I'd wait.
mistakes.v: Hypothetical: If I were you, I'd wait.

quiz.q: The committee insisted that the policy ___ reviewed annually.
quiz.e: Mandative subjunctive: insisted that it be reviewed.

quiz.q: It is vital that she ___ informed immediately.
quiz.e: It is vital that + base form: …that she be informed.

quiz.q: I wish it ___ possible to be in two places at once.
quiz.e: Wish + were-subjunctive: I wish it were possible.

grammar.title: Colons & dashes
grammar.lead: Colons introduce and dashes interrupt — both add sophistication when used precisely, and both are tested mercilessly in formal writing. Master the exact rules.

leadTr.uz: Ikki nuqta kiritadi, tire esa to'xtatadi — ikkalasi ham aniq ishlatilganda uslubni boyitadi. Aniq qoidalarni o'zlashtiring.
leadTr.ru: Двоеточие вводит, тире прерывает — оба знака делают стиль изящнее при точном использовании. Освойте точные правила.

quiz.q:
Text: 'The study identified three major risk factors[___] poor diet, sedentary lifestyle, and chronic stress.'

Which choice correctly completes the text?
quiz.e: An independent clause ('The study identified three major risk factors') followed by a list. D (:) correctly introduces the list. Both colon and dash would work, but in formal writing a colon is preferred.

quiz.q:
Text: 'The scientist[___]who had spent 30 years researching the topic[___]finally announced her breakthrough.'

Which choice correctly uses dashes?
quiz.e: 'Who had spent 30 years researching the topic' is parenthetical information. Em dashes must appear in PAIRS: 'The scientist—who had spent 30 years...—finally announced.' D is correct.

quiz.q:
Text: 'Her conclusion was simple[___] the current model was fundamentally flawed.'

Which choice correctly completes the text?
quiz.e: 'Her conclusion was simple' is an independent clause. A colon or dash can introduce the explanation that follows. D (:) is correct (formal). C (—) also works. Both D and C are valid — D is preferred in formal contexts.

quiz.q:
Text: 'The award[___]which had never before been given to a non-citizen[___]recognized her lifetime contributions.'

Which choice correctly uses dashes?
quiz.e: Em dashes must appear in PAIRS around parenthetical information. B (dash and dash) is correct: 'The award—which had never...non-citizen—recognized...'

quiz.q:
Text: 'The new policy accomplished one crucial thing[___]it gave low-income families access to affordable healthcare.'

Which choice correctly completes the text?
quiz.e: 'The new policy accomplished one crucial thing' is a complete independent clause. A colon introduces the explanation. C (:) is correct. D (em dash) would also work. Both are valid; C is the formal choice.

quiz.q:
Text: 'Three cities were considered for the summit[___]Geneva, Singapore, and Nairobi.'

Which choice correctly completes the text?
quiz.e: Complete independent clause followed by a list. D (:) is correct. C (—) would also work but the colon is more formal.

quiz.q:
Text: 'The expedition[___]the first of its kind in over fifty years[___]attracted international media attention.'

Which choice correctly uses dashes?
quiz.e: Parenthetical information in the middle of a sentence requires em dashes in PAIRS. C (dash and dash) is correct.

quiz.q:
Text: 'One conclusion emerged from the data[___]the intervention was only effective for adolescents.'

Which choice correctly completes the text?
quiz.e: Complete clause + explanation. C (:) is correct. B (—) also works. C preferred in formal writing.

quiz.q:
Text: 'The architect designed three landmark buildings[___]the concert hall, the public library, and the civic center.'

Which choice correctly completes the text?
quiz.e: Complete clause followed by a list of explanatory items. C (:) is correct. B (—) also works.

quiz.q:
Text: 'The company's success depended on[___]innovation, strategic partnerships, and market timing.'

Which choice correctly completes the text?
quiz.e: Colon CANNOT follow a preposition ('on'). D (no punctuation) is correct: 'depended on innovation, strategic partnerships, and market timing.'

quiz.q:
Text: 'The finding had one major implication[___]the standard treatment needed to be revised.'

Which choice correctly completes the text?
quiz.e: Complete clause + implication explained. C (:) is correct. B (—) also valid. C is formal choice.

quiz.q:
Text: 'The committee was divided[___]half supported the proposal, and half opposed it.'

Which choice correctly completes the text?
quiz.e: 'The committee was divided' is a complete clause. A colon introduces an explanation. B (:) is correct. A (em dash) would also work.

grammar.title: Apostrophes & possession
grammar.lead: Its or it's? Students' or student's? The apostrophe is small but ruthless. These exercises cover possession, contractions and the classic traps.

leadTr.uz: Its yoki it's? Students' yoki student's? Apostrof kichik, lekin shafqatsiz. Bu mashqlar egalik, qisqartma va klassik tuzoqlarni qamrab oladi.
leadTr.ru: Its или it's? Students' или student's? Апостроф мал, но беспощаден. Здесь — принадлежность, сокращения и классические ловушки.

quiz.q:
Text: 'The company released [___] annual sustainability report last month.'

Which choice correctly completes the text?
quiz.e: 'Its' = possessive (belonging to the company). Expand test: 'released it is annual report' → nonsense → use 'its' (no apostrophe). B is correct.

quiz.q:
Text: 'The professors [___] lectures on quantum mechanics attracted students from across the university.'

Which choice correctly completes the text?
quiz.e: Multiple professors → plural → plural possessive: 'professors'' (apostrophe after the s). B is correct. A would mean one professor. C doubles the s — never correct.

quiz.q:
Text: 'The researcher presented [___] findings to a panel of international experts.'

Which choice correctly completes the text?
quiz.e: 'Hers' is already a possessive pronoun — no apostrophe needed. C is correct. 'Her's' and 'hers'' are not real words.

quiz.q:
Text: 'Despite [___] best efforts, the team could not replicate the original experiment's results.'

Which choice correctly completes the text?
quiz.e: 'Their' = possessive pronoun (belonging to them). B is correct. A = they are. C = location. D is the expanded form of A.

quiz.q:
Text: 'The study examined the [___] responses to the new curriculum across three age groups.'

Which choice correctly completes the text?
quiz.e: 'Children' is an irregular plural (does not end in s). Possessive = add 's: 'children's.' A is correct.

quiz.q:
Text: 'The committee reviewed all six [___] proposals before making its final decision.'

Which choice correctly completes the text?
quiz.e: Multiple candidates (all six) → plural possessive: 'candidates'' (apostrophe after s). B is correct.

quiz.q:
Text: 'The [___] new initiative focuses on reducing carbon emissions.'

Which choice correctly completes the text?
quiz.e: One government → singular possessive: 'government's.' A is correct.

quiz.q:
Text: '[___] been over a decade since the discovery was first announced.'

Which choice correctly completes the text?
quiz.e: 'It's been...' = 'It has been...' — a contraction. B (it's) is correct. A (its) is possessive, not a contraction.

quiz.q:
Text: 'The scientist [___] research on deep-sea organisms earned her international recognition.'

Which choice correctly completes the text?
quiz.e: 'Whose' = possessive relative pronoun (the scientist's research). B is correct. A (who's) = 'who is' — expand test: 'the scientist who is research...' → nonsense.

quiz.q:
Text: 'The two [___] offices share the same building but operate completely independently.'

Which choice correctly completes the text?
quiz.e: Two departments → plural → plural possessive: 'departments'' (apostrophe after s). B is correct.

quiz.q:
Text: 'The [___] impact on the local ecosystem was studied for three years.'

Which choice correctly completes the text?
quiz.e: Multiple factories (implied by context) → plural possessive: 'factories'' (apostrophe after s, irregular plural formed with -ies). A is correct.

quiz.q:
Text: 'The company announced that [___] expanding operations to three new markets.'

Which choice correctly completes the text?
quiz.e: 'It's expanding' = 'it is expanding' — a contraction. B (it's) is correct.

grammar.title: Sentence boundaries
grammar.lead: Run-ons and fragments are the two ways a sentence can fail. Learn to detect where one complete thought ends and the next must begin.

leadTr.uz: Qo'shilib ketgan gaplar va chala gaplar — gap buzilishining ikki yo'li. Bitta to'liq fikr qayerda tugashini va keyingisi qayerda boshlanishi kerakligini aniqlashni o'rganing.
leadTr.ru: Слипшиеся предложения и фрагменты — два способа сломать предложение. Учитесь видеть, где заканчивается одна законченная мысль и должна начаться следующая.

quiz.q: Which version is a comma splice?
o: The data was compelling, so the board approved the project immediately.
The data was compelling; the board approved the project immediately.
The data was compelling, the board approved the project immediately.
Because the data was compelling, the board approved the project immediately.
quiz.e: B joins two independent clauses with only a comma — a comma splice.

quiz.q: Which version is a run-on?
o: The weather delayed the launch, and engineers rescheduled for the following week.
The weather delayed the launch engineers rescheduled for the following week.
Although the weather delayed the launch, engineers rescheduled for the following week.
The weather delayed the launch; engineers rescheduled for the following week.
quiz.e: B has two independent clauses with no punctuation or connector — a fused run-on.

quiz.q:
Text: 'The novel received mixed reviews upon publication[___] it is now considered a masterpiece of twentieth-century literature.'

Which choice correctly completes the text?
quiz.e: Two contrasting independent clauses. '; however,' correctly shows contrast with semicolon before and comma after.

quiz.q: Which version is a sentence fragment?
o: The scientist published her findings last month.
The board reviewed all proposals carefully.
quiz.e: B — 'After years of painstaking research' — is a dependent clause with no main clause. Fragment.

quiz.q:
Text: 'Solar panels have become significantly cheaper over the past decade[___] many households that previously could not afford them can now install them.'

Which choice correctly completes the text?
quiz.e: Two independent clauses. C (semicolon) correctly joins them. A = comma splice. D = run-on.

quiz.q: Which version correctly fixes the fragment 'Discovered in a remote cave in southern France'?
o: The paintings, discovered in a remote cave in southern France, date back 30,000 years.
Discovered in a remote cave in southern France the paintings date back 30,000 years.
Discovered in a remote cave in southern France, to date back 30,000 years.
Discovered in a remote cave in southern France; the paintings date back 30,000 years.
quiz.e: B attaches the participial phrase to the main sentence: 'The paintings... date back 30,000 years.' Correct sentence structure.

quiz.q:
Text: 'The researchers worked around the clock[___] they were determined to publish before the competing team.'

Which choice correctly completes the text?
quiz.e: Two independent clauses. C (semicolon) is correct. A = comma splice. D = run-on.

quiz.q: Which version is a fragment?
o: After the team analyzed all available data, it reached a conclusion.
The team analyzed all available data and reached a conclusion.
Having analyzed all available data, the team reached a definitive conclusion.
quiz.e: B is only a participial phrase — no subject, no main verb. Fragment.

quiz.q:
Text: 'The population has been declining for years[___] conservationists have been unable to determine the primary cause.'

Which choice correctly completes the text?
quiz.e: Contrast: declining but cause unknown. '; yet,' shows contrast with proper semicolon + comma punctuation.

quiz.q: Which version is NOT a fragment?
o: Although the researchers worked for three years.
The test results were inconclusive, but the study continued.
To determine the cause of the anomaly.
Because the test results were inconclusive.
quiz.e: C has a subject ('the study') and a main verb ('continued'). A, B are dependent clauses alone. D is an infinitive phrase alone.

quiz.q:
Text: 'The bridge was structurally sound[___] city engineers ordered it closed after residents reported unusual vibrations.'

Which choice correctly completes the text?
quiz.e: Sound but still closed — contrast. '; nevertheless,' correctly shows the contrast.

quiz.q: Which version correctly rewrites 'The experiment was a success. Which proved that the hypothesis was correct.' to eliminate the fragment?
o: The experiment was a success; which proved that the hypothesis was correct.
The experiment was a success, it proved that the hypothesis was correct.
The experiment was a success. That proved that the hypothesis was correct.
The experiment was a success, which proved that the hypothesis was correct.
quiz.e: A attaches 'which proved...' as a nonrestrictive relative clause — no longer a fragment. B incorrectly uses semicolon before a relative clause (not an independent clause). D is a comma splice.

grammar.title: Modifiers & parallelism
grammar.lead: 'Walking to work, the rain started' — who was walking? Dangling modifiers and broken parallel structures are subtle errors that mark the difference between B2 and C1 writing.

leadTr.uz: 'Walking to work, the rain started' — kim yurayotgan edi? Noto'g'ri bog'langan aniqlovchilar va buzilgan parallel tuzilmalar B2 va C1 yozuvini ajratib turadigan nozik xatolardir.
leadTr.ru: 'Walking to work, the rain started' — кто шёл? Висячие обороты и нарушенный параллелизм — тонкие ошибки, отличающие письмо C1 от B2.

quiz.q: Which version correctly fixes the dangling modifier?
o: The samples, returning from the field, were carefully labeled.
Returning from the field, the samples were carefully labeled by the team.
The team's samples returning from the field were carefully labeled.
Returning from the field, the team carefully labeled the samples.
quiz.e: 'Returning from the field' — who returned? The team. Subject after comma must be 'the team.' B is correct.

quiz.q: Which version is correctly parallel?
o: The CEO was praised for her vision, her work ethic, and her willingness to take bold risks.
The CEO was praised for having vision, her work ethic, and taking bold risks.
The CEO was praised for her vision, her work ethic, and taking bold risks.
The CEO was praised for vision, her work ethic, and that she took bold risks.
quiz.e: B: three parallel noun phrases — 'her vision, her work ethic, her willingness.' All possessive noun phrases. A mixes nouns and a gerund. C and D mix forms.

quiz.q: Which version corrects the dangling modifier 'Having examined the patient, the diagnosis was made'?
o: Having examined the patient, the diagnosis was made.
The patient, having been examined, the diagnosis was made.
A diagnosis was made, having examined the patient.
Having examined the patient, the doctor made a diagnosis.
quiz.e: 'Having examined the patient' — the doctor examined. B: subject after comma = 'the doctor.' Correct.

quiz.q: Which version is NOT correctly parallel?
o: She enjoys reading novels, watching films, and hiking trails.
He is talented, dedicated, and works very hard.
The course covers theory, practice, and application.
The study was comprehensive, rigorous, and well-documented.
quiz.e: B mixes adjectives (talented, dedicated) with a verb phrase (works very hard). Should be: 'talented, dedicated, and hardworking.'

quiz.q: Which placement of 'nearly' gives the meaning that almost all homes were affected?
o: The storm destroyed every home nearly in the neighborhood.
Nearly the storm destroyed every home in the neighborhood.
The storm nearly destroyed every home in the neighborhood.
The storm destroyed nearly every home in the neighborhood.
quiz.e: B: 'nearly every home' — 'nearly' directly modifies 'every home.' A: 'nearly destroyed' means the storm came close to destroying. B is correct for the intended meaning.

quiz.q: Which version uses 'not only...but also' correctly?
o: The vaccine not only preventing the disease but also reduces its severity.
The vaccine not only prevents the disease but also it reduces severity.
The vaccine not only prevents the disease but also reducing its severity.
The vaccine not only prevents the disease but also reduces its severity.
quiz.e: B: 'not only PREVENTS...but also REDUCES' — both base verbs, parallel. A ends with a gerund. C begins with a gerund. D adds 'it' unnecessarily.

quiz.q: Which version corrects the misplaced modifier?
o: On paper plates, she served cake to the children.
She served to the children cake on paper plates.
She served cake on paper plates to the children.
She served cake to the children on paper plates.
quiz.e: 'On paper plates' should modify 'cake' (the cake was on paper plates, not the children). C: 'cake on paper plates to the children' — modifier is adjacent to 'cake.' Correct.

quiz.q: Which version corrects the dangling modifier 'Written during the Great Depression, readers found the novel deeply moving'?
o: Readers found the novel, written during the Great Depression, deeply moving.
Written during the Great Depression, readers found the novel deeply moving.
Written during the Great Depression, the novel was found deeply moving by readers.
The novel, written during the Great Depression, readers found deeply moving.
quiz.e: 'Written during the Great Depression' modifies 'the novel.' C places the modifier immediately after 'the novel' as a nonrestrictive element — correct. B also works. C is cleaner.

quiz.q: Which version makes a correct parallel comparison?
o: Both B and C are correct.
The population of Tokyo is larger than New York's.
The population of Tokyo is larger than New York.
The population of Tokyo is larger than the population of New York.
quiz.e: B (Tokyo's population vs. New York's) and C (Tokyo's population vs. New York's population) both correctly compare population to population. D is correct.

quiz.q: Which correctly fixes the dangling modifier 'To pass the course, regular attendance is required'?
o: Both B and C are correct.
To pass the course, students must attend regularly.
To pass the course, regular attendance is required.
Regular attendance is required to pass the course.
quiz.e: A is a dangling modifier (attendance doesn't pass courses; students do). B fixes the subject. C restructures. Both B and C are correct. D is the answer.

quiz.q: 'The scientist observed the samples using a high-powered microscope.' The modifier 'using a high-powered microscope' is ambiguous. Which revision is clearest?
o: Using a high-powered microscope, the scientist observed the samples.
Using a high-powered microscope, the samples were observed by the scientist.
The scientist, using a high-powered microscope, observed the samples.
Both B and C are correct.
quiz.e: B and C both correctly attach 'using a high-powered microscope' to 'the scientist' (the person using the microscope). Both are clear and grammatically correct. D is the answer.

quiz.q: Which version uses 'both...and' correctly?
o: The policy is both controversial and wide criticism has followed.
The policy is both controversial and widely criticized.
The policy is both controversial and it has been widely criticized.
The policy both is controversial and widely criticized.
quiz.e: B: 'both CONTROVERSIAL and WIDELY CRITICIZED' — both adjective phrases parallel. A mixes adjective and clause. C is awkward. D mixes adjective and clause.

grammar.title: Words in context
grammar.lead: Advanced texts choose words for precision, not decoration. Use the logic of the passage — contrast, cause, tone — to select the word that fits exactly.

leadTr.uz: Murakkab matnlar so'zni bezak uchun emas, aniqlik uchun tanlaydi. Matn mantig'idan — qarama-qarshilik, sabab, ohang — foydalanib, aynan mos so'zni tanlang.
leadTr.ru: Сложные тексты выбирают слова ради точности, а не украшения. Опирайтесь на логику текста — контраст, причину, тон — чтобы выбрать точное слово.

quiz.q:
Text: 'Critics have questioned whether canonical works of Western literature adequately represent human diversity, or whether the canon merely reflects the prejudices of those who codified it.'

As used in the text, 'codified' most nearly means
o: arranged into a systematic body of rules or standards
quiz.e: The canon was 'codified' — established and systematized into a recognized body of works. 'Codified' = arranged into a formal system or set of standards.

quiz.q:
Text: 'The speaker's tone was measured throughout the debate, conveying neither the contempt her critics expected nor the enthusiasm her supporters hoped for.'

As used in the text, 'measured' most nearly means
quiz.e: The tone was moderate — neither contemptuous nor enthusiastic. 'Measured' here = carefully controlled and restrained. 'Quantified' is a different sense entirely.

quiz.q:
Text: 'The proposed reforms enjoyed broad popular support but faced sustained resistance from entrenched interests in the legislature who stood to lose influence if the changes were implemented.'

As used in the text, 'entrenched' most nearly means
o: firmly established and resistant to change
quiz.e: 'Entrenched interests' = deeply established and resistant to change. They've long held their positions. 'Recently installed' is the opposite meaning.

quiz.q:
Text: 'The novelist's prose style has been described as austere, stripped of ornamentation and reliant on plain declarative sentences that place the weight of meaning on individual words.'

As used in the text, 'austere' most nearly means
quiz.e: 'Austere' prose is stripped of ornamentation — severely simple. B captures this. 'Morally rigorous' applies to people or conduct, not prose style.

quiz.q:
Text: 'The startup's rapid expansion was celebrated, but observers who scrutinized its financial filings noted that profitability remained elusive despite record revenue growth.'

As used in the text, 'elusive' most nearly means
quiz.e: Profitability 'remained elusive' despite efforts — it was not yet obtained. 'Elusive' = difficult to achieve or attain. 'Secretive' is wrong. 'Present in small amounts' is wrong.

quiz.q:
Text: 'The historian carefully distinguished between primary sources — documents produced at the time of the events — and secondary sources, which interpret and synthesize primary materials.'

As used in the text, 'synthesize' most nearly means
o: combine elements into a coherent whole
quiz.e: 'Synthesize primary materials' = combine and integrate them into a unified analysis. The chemistry meaning (produce artificially) doesn't apply in this academic writing context.

quiz.q:
Text: 'The administration's position on the treaty was ambiguous: official statements seemed to support ratification, but unnamed officials suggested the president harbored significant reservations.'

As used in the text, 'harbored' most nearly means
quiz.e: The president 'harbored reservations' = held or maintained them internally, without expressing them publicly. 'Concealed from authorities' implies illegality, which doesn't fit.

quiz.q:
Text: 'The peacock's elaborate tail is described as a 'costly signal' — a feature so metabolically expensive to produce that its very existence demonstrates the fitness of the individual bearing it.'

As used in the text, 'costly' most nearly means
quiz.e: 'Metabolically expensive' is the context — the passage itself clarifies the sense. 'Costly' here means requiring significant biological/metabolic resources, not money.

quiz.q:
Text: 'The scientist's reputation, once sterling, was tarnished by the revelation that several of her most celebrated findings could not be replicated by independent researchers.'

As used in the text, 'tarnished' most nearly means
quiz.e: 'Tarnished reputation' = damaged, made less bright — a metaphor from metal tarnishing. 'Completely destroyed' is too strong; the passage says 'tarnished,' not 'destroyed.'

quiz.q:
Text: 'The committee's findings were tentative, acknowledging that available data was insufficient to support definitive conclusions and calling for further investigation.'

As used in the text, 'tentative' most nearly means
quiz.e: 'Tentative findings' = preliminary, not fully established, open to revision. 'Not fully committed or certain' captures this. 'Intended as temporary' misses the certainty/confidence aspect.

quiz.q:
Text: 'The anthropologist argued that gift-giving in this culture was not merely ceremonial but served to articulate and reinforce complex social hierarchies among participants.'

As used in the text, 'articulate' most nearly means
o: express or give form to something
quiz.e: Gift-giving 'articulates' social hierarchies — expresses and makes them manifest. 'Speak clearly' is the adjective/adverb meaning applied to a person, not to a cultural practice.

quiz.q:
Text: 'The researcher noted that the initial findings were suggestive but not conclusive, warranting replication before they could be incorporated into clinical guidelines.'

As used in the text, 'warranting' most nearly means
quiz.e: The findings 'warrant replication' = require/justify replication before clinical use. 'Legally authorizing' is the legal warranty sense, which doesn't fit an academic context.

grammar.title: Concision & precision
grammar.lead: Strong English says more with fewer words. Spot redundancy, cut empty phrases, and keep the sentence's full meaning intact.

leadTr.uz: Kuchli ingliz tili kam so'z bilan ko'p ma'no beradi. Ortiqchalikni toping, bo'sh iboralarni olib tashlang, gapning to'liq ma'nosini saqlang.
leadTr.ru: Сильный английский говорит больше меньшим числом слов. Находите избыточность, убирайте пустые фразы, сохраняя полный смысл.

quiz.q:
Text: 'The council decided to postpone and delay the vote until a later date in the future.'

Which choice most effectively revises the sentence to eliminate unnecessary repetition?
o: The council decided to postpone the vote.
The council decided to later postpone and delay the vote.
The council decided to postpone and delay the vote to a future date.
The council decided to postpone and delay the vote until a later date in the future.
quiz.e: 'Postpone' and 'delay' are synonyms (redundant pair). 'Until a later date in the future' — 'later date' and 'in the future' both mean the same thing, and 'postpone' already implies moving to a future time. B keeps only the essential meaning.

quiz.q:
Text: 'The reason the project failed was because the team lacked adequate resources.'

Which choice most effectively revises the underlined portion?
o: The reason the project failed was that the team lacked adequate resources.
The reason for which the project failed was because the team lacked in adequate resources.
The reason the project failed was because the team lacked adequate resources.
The project failed due to the fact that there was a lack of adequate resources on the team.
quiz.e: 'The reason was because' is redundant — 'because' already introduces a reason. The correct form is 'the reason was that.' B makes this correction. A keeps the error. C adds 'due to the fact that' (wordy). D is grammatically awkward and keeps 'because.'

quiz.q:
Text: 'The completely exhausted marathon runners finally crossed the finish line at the end of the race.'

Which revision most effectively eliminates redundancy?
o: The marathon runners, who were exhausted, finally crossed the finish line at the end of the race.
The completely exhausted marathon runners finally crossed the finish line at the end of the race.
The completely exhausted and very tired marathon runners finally crossed the finish line at the end of the race.
The exhausted marathon runners crossed the finish line.
quiz.e: 'Completely exhausted' — 'completely' is a meaningless intensifier (you're either exhausted or you're not). 'At the end of the race' is implied by 'crossing the finish line.' B removes both. A keeps both. C adds 'and very tired' (redundant with exhausted). D keeps 'at the end of the race.'

quiz.q:
Text: 'Due to the fact that the medication has the ability to cause serious side effects, patients should consult their doctors.'

Which revision is most concise without losing meaning?
o: Because the medication can cause serious side effects, patients should consult their doctors.
Due to the fact that the medication has the ability to cause serious side effects, patients should consult their doctors.
As a result of the fact that the medication possesses the ability to cause serious side effects, patients should consult with their doctors.
The medication has the ability to cause serious side effects, which is the reason why patients should consult their doctors.
quiz.e: 'Due to the fact that' → 'because' | 'has the ability to' → 'can.' B applies both concisions. A keeps both wordy phrases. C replaces one wordy phrase with an even wordier one. D keeps 'has the ability to' and adds 'which is the reason why.'

quiz.q:
Text: 'Scientists made an unexpected and surprising discovery about the origins of the universe.'

Which revision eliminates the redundancy?
o: Scientists made a surprising discovery about the origins of the universe.
Scientists made an unexpected and surprising discovery about the origins of the universe.
Scientists made a very unexpected discovery that was surprising about the origins of the universe.
Scientists made a discovery that was both unexpected and also surprising about the origins of the universe.
quiz.e: 'Unexpected' and 'surprising' are synonyms when describing a discovery — a redundant pair. B keeps just 'surprising.' A keeps both. C adds 'very' and rephrases awkwardly. D adds 'both...and also' (more words, same redundancy).

quiz.q:
Text: 'The new policy will help facilitate the improvement of working conditions for employees at the company.'

Which is the most concise revision?
o: The new policy has the ability to help in the facilitation of improvements to employee working conditions.
The new policy will facilitate the improvement and betterment of working conditions for all employees at the company.
The new policy will help improve working conditions for employees.
The new policy will help facilitate the improvement of working conditions for employees at the company.
quiz.e: 'Help facilitate the improvement of' → 'help improve' (three words become two). 'At the company' is contextually implied when talking about a company policy. B is maximally concise. A is wordy. C adds 'betterment' (redundant with improvement). D is much wordier.

quiz.q:
Text: 'The ancient ruins, which were old and dated back thousands of years, attracted tourists from around the world.'

Which revision is most effective?
o: The ancient ruins, which were old and dated back thousands of years, attracted tourists from around the world.
The ancient ruins, which dated back thousands of years, attracted tourists from around the world.
The old, ancient ruins, which were thousands of years old, attracted tourists from around the world.
The ruins, which were ancient and dated back many thousands of years into the past, attracted tourists from around the world.
quiz.e: 'Ancient ruins which were old' — 'ancient' and 'old' are redundant. 'Dated back thousands of years' shows age, making 'which were old' doubly redundant. B removes 'which were old' and 'ancient' (keeping 'ancient' in the main noun is actually better than the clause). A keeps all redundancies. C has 'old, ancient' (redundant pair). D has 'many thousands of years into the past' ('into the past' is redundant with 'dated back').

quiz.q:
Text: 'In the event that the experiment produces unexpected results, researchers should document and record all observations.'

Which revision is most concise?
o: In the event that the experiment produces unexpected results, researchers need to make documentation and recordings of all observations.
Should the experiment produce results that are unexpected in nature, researchers ought to document and record their observations.
If the experiment produces unexpected results, researchers should document all observations.
In the event that the experiment produces unexpected results, researchers should document and record all observations.
quiz.e: 'In the event that' → 'if' (4 words → 1). 'Document and record' — redundant pair; 'document' includes recording. B applies both concisions. A keeps both. C adds 'in nature' and 'ought to document and record.' D keeps 'in the event that' and adds 'make documentation and recordings.'

quiz.q:
Text: 'The athlete was able to successfully complete the marathon in under three hours.'

Which revision eliminates the redundancy?
o: The athlete was able to and did successfully complete the marathon in under three hours.
The athlete was able to successfully complete the marathon in under three hours.
The athlete completed the marathon in under three hours.
The athlete was successful in being able to complete the marathon in a time under three hours.
quiz.e: 'Was able to' and 'successfully' are both implied by 'complete' — if you complete something, you were able to do it and you did it successfully. B strips both. A keeps both. C adds 'in a time under' (wordy). D adds 'and did.'

quiz.q:
Text: 'The report's findings were both important and significant to the future advancement of the field.'

Which is the most effective revision?
o: The report's findings were significant for the advancement of the field.
The report's findings were important, significant, and consequential for the future of the field.
The report's findings were both important and significant to the future advancement of the field.
The report's findings were very important and quite significant for the future advancement of the field.
quiz.e: 'Important and significant' — redundant pair. 'Future advancement' — 'advancement' implies moving forward (future is redundant). B removes the redundant pair and 'future.' A keeps both. C adds a third synonym ('consequential'). D adds intensifiers ('very,' 'quite').

quiz.q:
Text: 'The new bridge design incorporates several different features that are unique and one-of-a-kind.'

Which revision is most effective?
o: The new bridge design incorporates features that are unique, one-of-a-kind, and unlike any other.
The new bridge design, which is new, incorporates several different and varied unique features.
The new bridge design incorporates several unique features.
The new bridge design incorporates several different features that are unique and one-of-a-kind.
quiz.e: 'Different' is redundant with 'several' (several already implies differences). 'Unique' and 'one-of-a-kind' are synonyms. 'That are' is a wordy relative clause replaceable by an adjective. B strips all: 'several unique features.' A keeps all redundancies. C triples the synonyms. D adds 'which is new' (already in 'new bridge design') and 'different and varied.'

quiz.q:
Text: 'The novel is widely considered one of the greatest and most celebrated achievements in American literature.'

Which choice eliminates the redundancy most effectively?
o: one of the greatest, most celebrated, and most acclaimed achievements in American literature
one of the greatest achievements in American literature
one of the very greatest and widely celebrated achievements in American literature
one of the greatest and most celebrated achievements in American literature
quiz.e: 'Greatest' and 'most celebrated' overlap in meaning as superlative praise — using both is redundant. B keeps only 'greatest.' A keeps both. C adds a third ('most acclaimed'). D adds 'very' and 'widely.'
